title: Clients
content:
Clients # The server speaks RESP, so a Redis client works — with three adjustments: type mismatches never error, scan cursors must stay opaque, and there is no SELECT/MULTI.
redis-cli # redis-cli -h 127.0.0.1 -p 11001 # with TLS and auth redis-cli --tls --cacert ./ca.crt -a "$ICEFIREDB_AUTH" -h db1.internal -p 11001 SET user:1 '{"name":"ada"}' EX 300 HGETALL user:1 SCAN 0 MATCH 'user:*' COUNT 100 XSCAN HASH "" MATCH '^user:' COUNT 100 INFO redis-cli --scan works: it starts at 0 and loops until the cursor is 0 again.
Go (github.com/redis/go-redis/v9) # package main import ( "context" "crypto/tls" "fmt" "github.com/redis/go-redis/v9" ) func main() { ctx := context.Background() rdb := redis.NewClient(&redis.Options{ Addr: "127.0.0.1:11001", Password: "", // set when the server runs with --auth TLSConfig: nil, // &tls.Config{...} when --tls-cert/--tls-key are used DB: 0, // there is only database 0 }) defer rdb.Close() if err := rdb.Set(ctx, "user:1", `{"name":"ada"}`, 0).Err(); err != nil { panic(err) } v, err := rdb.Get(ctx, "user:1").Result() fmt.Println(v, err) // {"name":"ada"} <nil> fmt.Println(rdb.HSet(ctx, "user:1", "name", "ada").Val()) // 1 // Paginate keys: the cursor is opaque, handle it as a string. cursor := uint64(0) for { keys, next, err := rdb.Scan(ctx, cursor, "user:*", 100).Result() if err != nil { panic(err) } fmt.Println(keys) if next == 0 { break } cursor = next } } Caveat — typed scan helpers. rdb.HScan, rdb.SScan, rdb.ZScan and rdb.Scan all coerce the cursor through strconv.ParseUint, and HScan/SScan/ZScan additionally expect a numeric cursor. This engine returns the last field/member name as the cursor for those three, so the typed helpers fail with a parse error. Use the generic API instead:
cursor := "0" for { vals, err := rdb.Do(ctx, "HSCAN", "user:1", cursor, "MATCH", "n*", "COUNT", 100).Slice() if err != nil { panic(err) } cursor = fmt.Sprint(vals[0]) pairs := vals[1].([]interface{}) for i := 0; i+1 < len(pairs); i += 2 { fmt.Println(pairs[i], pairs[i+1]) } if cursor == "0" || cursor == "" { break } } redis.NewClusterClient also works: CLUSTER SLOTS reports one range covering 0-16383 on the leader, which is a valid single-shard topology. It is pointless for distribution, useful for client uniformity — and it follows -MOVED redirects automatically.
Python (redis-py) # import redis r = redis.Redis( host="127.0.0.1", port=11001, password=None, # set when the server runs with --auth ssl=False, # True with --tls-cert/--tls-key decode_responses=True, ) r.set("user:1", '{"name":"ada"}') print(r.get("user:1")) print(r.hset("user:1", "name", "ada")) print(r.ttl("user:1")) # works: TTL is per type # The typed helpers coerce the cursor to int, which this engine's cursors are not. cursor = "0" while True: cursor, pairs = r.execute_command("HSCAN", "user:1", cursor, "COUNT", 100) print(pairs) if cursor in ("0", b"0"): break Node (ioredis) # const Redis = require("ioredis"); const r = new Redis({ host: "127.0.0.1", port: 11001 /*, password, tls: {} */ }); (async () => { await r.set("user:1", '{"name":"ada"}'); console.log(await r.get("user:1")); console.log(await r.hset("user:1", "name", "ada")); // hscan returns [cursor, flatArray]; ioredis keeps the cursor as a string let [cursor, flat] = await r.hscan("user:1", "0", "COUNT", 100); while (cursor !== "0") { [cursor, flat] = await r.hscan("user:1", cursor, "COUNT", 100); } })(); Standard caveats # Caveat What to do No WRONGTYPE Enforce type rules in a key-naming convention or in the application No TYPE command Track the type yourself; or probe with EXISTS/HKEYEXISTS/LKEYEXISTS/SKEYEXISTS No SELECT Set DB: 0 and forget about it No MULTI/EXEC Use SET … NX for atomic claims, BARRIER for read-your-writes No BLPOP Poll LPOP, or use a queue designed for blocking reads HGET/GET of an empty value returns null on P2P drivers Store a sentinel when “empty” must survive Follower reads need --openreads Without it, expect -MOVED 0 <leader> INFO takes no arguments Parse the single reply; do not call INFO memory Health from a client # redis-cli -p 11001 PING # PONG when the process is up redis-cli -p 11001 BARRIER # OK once this client's writes are applied redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT LEADER # who to write to curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:11002/readyz # 200 "ready" once storage is initialized

title: Configuration
content:
Configuration # The NoSQL engine has no configuration file. Every setting is a command-line flag, parsed once at startup in flags.go. (A .env file in the working directory is loaded as well — see Environment variables.)
./bin/IceFireDB -h # prints the usage block below Basic options # Flag Meaning Default -a addr Bind address (host:port) 127.0.0.1:11001 -n id Node ID — also the Raft server ID and the data subdirectory name 1 -d dir Data directory data -j addr Leader address of a cluster to join (empty — bootstrap) -l level Log level: debug, verb, info, warn, silent info -h Print usage and exit — -n is an identifier, not a port. Ports come from -a. Two nodes may share -d because each one writes to <dir>/IceFireDB/<node-id>/, but two nodes must not share a node ID.
Security options # Flag Meaning Default --auth token Cluster authorization token, shared by all nodes and all clients (empty — auth disabled) --tls-cert path TLS certificate (PEM) (empty) --tls-key path TLS private key (PEM) (empty) --tls-cert and --tls-key must be supplied together; supplying one without the other is a startup error. --auth is also accepted from ICEFIREDB_AUTH, and the command-line flag wins when both are set. Full behaviour, including what the token does and does not protect, is in Security.
Cluster and networking options # Flag Meaning Default --advertise addr Address other nodes should use to reach this one (network bound address) --openreads Let followers serve read commands (possibly stale) false --nosync Skip the per-write disk sync (faster, loses recent writes on power loss) false --localtime Take the Raft clock from the local machine instead of the network time source false --try-errors Answer -TRY instead of -MOVED for non-leader reads, and disable the CLUSTER command false --restore path Bootstrap a brand-new single-node cluster from a snapshot file (empty) --init-run-quit Initialize the bootstrap state and exit false --raft-backend name Raft log store: leveldb or bolt leveldb --advertise must include a port; a value without one (or with a non-numeric port) is rejected at startup. --restore cannot be combined with -j, and is ignored when the data directory already exists. See Clustering and Operations.
Storage options # Flag Meaning Default --storage-backend name KV driver behind the ledis data model goleveldb --ipfs-endpoint url IPFS API endpoint (HTTP API, not a gateway) http://localhost:5001 --ipfs-synckv-key key Encryption key for the ipfs-synckv driver (AES-256: 32 bytes) (empty — no encryption) --ipfs-log-dbname name Database name/identifier shared by ipfs-log nodes ifdb-event-kv-ipfs-log --oss-endpoint url S3-compatible endpoint http://localhost:9000 --oss-ak key Access key placeholder value in the driver default --oss-sk secret Secret key placeholder value in the driver default Supported --storage-backend values: goleveldb, badger, hybriddb, oss, ipfs, ipfs-synckv, crdt, ipfs-log. leveldb (the cgo driver) and orbitdb are not compiled into the binary. See Storage backends for what each driver guarantees.
P2P options (decentralized drivers) # These configure the libp2p layer used by the crdt and ipfs-log drivers. They have no effect on the local and object-store drivers.
Flag Meaning Default --servicename name Service-discovery identifier icefiredb --nettopic topic Node-discovery pubsub channel icefiredb-net --datatopic topic Data-synchronisation pubsub channel icefiredb-data Nodes only exchange data when all three match. Changing them on a live cluster splits it.
Observability options # Flag Meaning Default --metrics Enable the HTTP endpoints /healthz, /readyz, /metrics false --metrics-addr addr Bind address for those endpoints 127.0.0.1:11002 --pprof Enable the pprof profiling server false --pprof-addr addr pprof bind address 127.0.0.1:26063 Both servers are off by default and bound to loopback on purpose. See Observability.
Diagnostic options # Flag Meaning Default -t 1..9 Test helper: derive address and node ID from a single digit (node 1 bootstraps, the rest join it) (unset) --debug Registered but currently unused false -t is a local-cluster convenience; it is not part of the documented interface and rewrites -a, -n and -j.
Environment variables # Variable Read by Effect ICEFIREDB_AUTH flags.go Cluster auth token when --auth is not on the command line IPFS_LOG_DBNAME driver/ipfs-log Overrides the ipfs-log database name at open time The binary also calls godotenv.Load() at startup, so a .env file in the working directory can set the variables above. Keep secrets in ICEFIREDB_AUTH or .env rather than on the command line — the process list is world-readable on most systems.
Flags that are printed but not wired # -h prints a Store options line for --hot-cache-size. That flag is not registered and has no effect: the hot-cache capacity of the oss, ipfs and ipfs-synckv drivers is the driver default of 1024 MB, set in driver/*/db.go. The same is true of --pubsub-id, which is in the usage text but commented out with the disabled OrbitDB driver.
Passing an unregistered flag makes Go’s flag package terminate with flag provided but not defined, so this is visible immediately rather than silently ignored.
--debug is the opposite case: it is registered, but nothing reads the variable it sets, so it changes nothing either.
Recipes # Local development, one node
./bin/IceFireDB -a 127.0.0.1:11001 -n 1 -d ./data -l debug --nosync Three-node cluster with auth and metrics on loopback
export ICEFIREDB_AUTH=change-me ./bin/IceFireDB -n 1 -a 0.0.0.0:11001 --advertise 10.0.0.1:11001 -d /var/lib/icefiredb --metrics ./bin/IceFireDB -n 2 -a 0.0.0.0:11001 --advertise 10.0.0.2:11001 -d /var/lib/icefiredb --metrics -j 10.0.0.1:11001 ./bin/IceFireDB -n 3 -a 0.0.0.0:11001 --advertise 10.0.0.3:11001 -d /var/lib/icefiredb --metrics -j 10.0.0.1:11001 Badger, TLS, and follower reads
./bin/IceFireDB --storage-backend badger --tls-cert ./cert.pem --tls-key ./key.pem \ --openreads -a 0.0.0.0:11001 -d /var/lib/icefiredb Decentralized CRDT driver
./bin/IceFireDB --storage-backend crdt \ --servicename my-service --nettopic my-net --datatopic my-data \ -d /var/lib/icefiredb

title: Overview
content:
Engine overview # Startup sequence # main() does a small, fixed amount of work, and the ordering matters:
godotenv.Load() — pick up .env if present. confInit(&conf) — parse flags, resolve --auth from the environment, validate TLS pairing and --advertise, map --raft-backend to leveldb/bolt. conf.DataDirReady is registered as a callback: when the Raft layer has prepared the node directory it opens the storage backend (openStorage) and publishes ldb. The command handlers only work after this point, which is why /readyz exists. Backend metrics are registered with the INFO collector (hybriddb, ipfs, ipfs-synckv). --pprof and --metrics servers start, if enabled — both are plain net/http servers in goroutines. conf.Snapshot/Restore are wired to snapshot.go, connection hooks to the client counter, and rafthub.Main(conf) takes over: recover the log, join a cluster if -j was given, serve RESP. Request path # Writes (the 56 commands registered with AddWriteCommand):
client → RESP parse → normalise (lowercase command name, args to strings) → leader check → append to Raft log → replicate → commit at quorum → apply on every node in log order → handler → ledis → driver The handler executes during apply, not before the append, which is what makes the same result appear on every node. A handler that reads the wall clock or math/rand would therefore diverge — it must use m.Now()/m.Rand(), whose values are themselves replicated through the internal TICK command.
Reads (the 54 commands registered with AddReadCommand):
client → RESP parse → (openreads? local : leader) → handler → ledis → driver A leader serves reads after ensuring its applied index covers the client’s own earlier writes. A follower either answers -MOVED 0 <leader> or, with --openreads, serves what it has applied.
System commands (RAFT, CLUSTER, MACHINE, BARRIER) bypass the data space and talk to the Raft wrapper directly.
Components and where they live # Layer Implementation Files RESP server, pipelining, auth, Raft tidwall/uhaha + tidwall/redcon vendor/github.com/tidwall/uhaha Data model, per-type keyspaces, TTLs ledisdb/ledis vendor/github.com/ledisdb/ledisdb/ledis Command handlers this repository strings.go, hashes.go, lists.go, set.go, sorted_sets.go, scan.go, servers.go Storage drivers this repository + ledis driver/*, vendor/.../store/goleveldb Snapshots this repository snapshot.go Observability this repository + Prometheus client observability.go, server_info.go Process model # One process, one goroutine per connection, one Raft apply loop. There is no per-command thread pool and no internal partitioning: a slow command blocks the apply loop, which is why LINSERT/LREM are documented as O(n) hazards and BLPOP is not implemented at all.
Failure domains # Failure Blast radius A handler returns an error mid-write The command fails; earlier applied writes stay applied (no rollback) Backend write fails during a list rebuild The list is left truncated (LINSERT/LREM) Process crash Uncommitted log entries are lost; committed entries are recovered from store/ Node disk loss The node rejoins from the leader’s log/snapshot; the cluster is unaffected while a majority lives Majority loss Writes stop (-CLUSTERDOWN); reads with --openreads continue What is deliberately not here # No sharding, no SQL engine, no secondary indexes, no scripting, no pub/sub, no streams, no transactions, no vector search. Element stores (IceFireDB-PubSub, the SQL proxies) are separate binaries in this repository, not features of this one.

title: Strings
content:
Strings # 26 commands: the SET family, counters, bit operations and string expiry.
Cmd RW Syntax Returns Example → reply SET W SET KEY VALUE [EX seconds] [PX milliseconds] [NX] [XX] [KEEPTTL] +OK, or null when NX/XX blocks the write SET user:1 '{"n":"ada"}' EX 60 → OK SETNX W SETNX KEY VALUE integer 1 written, 0 already exists SETNX job:42 1 → 1 SETEX W SETEX KEY seconds VALUE +OK SETEX session:9 60 tok → OK SETEXAT W SETEXAT KEY unixTime VALUE +OK SETEXAT session:9 1767225600 tok → OK GETSET W GETSET KEY VALUE bulk old value, null if absent GETSET counter 0 → "7" GET R GET KEY bulk, null if absent GET user:1 → {"n":"ada"} MGET R MGET KEY [KEY ...] array of bulk/null MGET a b → [val, null] MSET W MSET KEY VALUE [KEY VALUE ...] +OK MSET a 1 b 2 → OK APPEND W APPEND KEY VALUE integer new length APPEND log "x\n" → 5 STRLEN R STRLEN KEY integer length in bytes STRLEN user:1 → 13 INCR W INCR KEY integer new value INCR hits → 1 INCRBY W INCRBY KEY increment integer new value INCRBY hits 5 → 6 DECR W DECR KEY integer new value DECR hits → 5 DECRBY W DECRBY KEY decrement integer new value DECRBY hits 5 → 0 GETRANGE R GETRANGE KEY start end bulk substring (inclusive, negative offsets from the end) GETRANGE user:1 0 3 → {"n" SETRANGE W SETRANGE KEY offset VALUE integer new length SETRANGE user:1 0 '{"m"' → 13 GETBIT R GETBIT KEY offset integer 0/1 GETBIT bitmap 7 → 0 SETBIT W SETBIT KEY offset value integer previous bit SETBIT bitmap 7 1 → 0 BITCOUNT R BITCOUNT KEY [start end [BYTE|BIT]] integer number of set bits BITCOUNT bitmap 0 0 → 1 BITOP W BITOP AND|OR|XOR|NOT destKey KEY [KEY ...] integer length of the result BITOP AND out a b → 2 BITPOS R BITPOS KEY bit [start [end [BYTE|BIT]]] integer position, -1 if not found BITPOS bitmap 1 → 7 DEL W DEL KEY [KEY ...] integer keys removed DEL a b → 2 EXISTS R EXISTS KEY [KEY ...] integer number of existing keys EXISTS a b → 1 EXPIRE W EXPIRE KEY seconds integer 1 set, 0 key absent EXPIRE session:9 60 → 1 EXPIREAT W EXPIREAT KEY unixTime integer 1 set, 0 key absent EXPIREAT session:9 1767225600 → 1 TTL R TTL KEY integer seconds left, -1 no expiration TTL session:9 → 59 Notes # SET clears an existing expiration unless KEEPTTL is given. PX is rounded up to the next second because expirations are stored in whole seconds, so PX 500 keeps the key 1 s and PX 1500 keeps it 2 s — never less than asked. SET ... NX/XX answers a null bulk when the condition blocks the write, not an error. There is no string PERSIST: the handler exists but is commented out and not registered. To keep a value and change its lifetime, EXPIRE again or use SET … KEEPTTL. EXISTS counts keys in the string keyspace only; it will not see a hash with the same name. Use HKEYEXISTS, LKEYEXISTS, SKEYEXISTS for the other types. DEL deletes the string at those keys, not the same-named hash/list/set. INCR/DECR on a non-numeric value answer -ERR, like Redis; a missing key is treated as 0. BITCOUNT/BITPOS accept the optional BYTE/BIT unit as in Redis 7. Expiry arithmetic uses the Raft clock, so a short TTL can be rejected on a node whose Raft clock lags its local clock. See Compatibility. TTL is computed against the local wall clock by the storage layer, so replicas can report values that differ by their apply latency.

title: Building and testing
content:
Building and testing # Build # make localbuild # bin/IceFireDB for the host platform make run # go run . (development) make run_dev # same, for a dev setup make clean # remove bin/ and installed copies Release and cross-compilation targets exist (make all, make release, make build-linux-*), but while iterating on the code use run/localbuild — the release matrix builds five GOOS/GOARCH variants per invocation.
The binary embeds its git revision and build time:
go build -ldflags "-X main.BuildVersion=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) -X main.BuildDate=$(date '+%F %T')" -o bin/IceFireDB . -h shows the version and, when BuildVersion is set, includes it in the banner.
Test suites # Command What it runs make test / go test ./... Unit tests, honouring DRIVER DRIVER=goleveldb make test-compat RESP compatibility suite, -tags alltest make test-integration Builds the binary, then crash-recovery and multi-node Raft failover tests (-tags integration) make test-partition Docker-based split-brain test: 3 nodes, leader cut off the network (-tags partition) make soak Sustained load against a 3-node cluster; SOAK_DURATION, SOAK_WORKERS, SOAK_CHAOS=1 DRIVER selects the storage backend the tests exercise (badger is the Makefile default):
DRIVER=badger make test DRIVER=goleveldb make test-compat DRIVER=hybriddb go test ./driver/hybriddb/... Some drivers need infrastructure before their tests can run:
Driver Requirement oss S3-compatible endpoint; CI starts LocalStack and sets OSS_TEST_ENDPOINT ipfs, ipfs-synckv IPFS daemon at --ipfs-endpoint crdt, ipfs-log libp2p connectivity between test nodes What CI runs # .github/workflows/test.yml runs the alltest suite once per driver — oss, ipfs, ipfs-synckv, goleveldb, crdt, ipfs-log, badger, hybriddb — plus driver-specific packages and the SQLite suite. The oss job uses LocalStack (MinIO’s public image no longer pulls anonymously).
.github/workflows/build.yml builds the five release targets, so a change that only compiles on amd64 does not sneak through.
Both workflows pin the toolchain the module declares: go 1.26.0 with toolchain go1.27.3, and CI runs Go 1.27.3. A local go older than that will fail on the module’s toolchain directive rather than on the code.
Writing a test for a command # //go:build alltest package main import ( "context" "testing" ) func TestMyCommandContract(t *testing.T) { c := getTestConn() // helper used by the compat suite ctx := context.Background() // 1. the happy path // 2. the boundary the handler is supposed to enforce // 3. the reply type, not just the value _ = c _ = ctx } The compatibility suite is the right place for anything that pins a divergence from Redis, because compat_test.go is the document those divergences point at.
Static checks worth running by hand # go vet ./... gofmt -l . # expect no output outside vendor/ go mod tidy && go mod vendor # after touching go.mod Note that go mod vendor rewrites the vendor/ tree — the Raft/RESP layer and ledis live there, so a vendor update is a code review, not a formality.

title: Clustering
content:
Clustering # A cluster is a set of nodes that share one Raft log. Every write command is appended to that log and replayed by every node, so all nodes converge on the same state; reads are answered locally by whichever node receives them.
Bootstrapping and joining # The first node needs no extra flag: an empty -j means “start a new cluster”. Every later node joins with -j <leader-or-any-node-address>:
./bin/IceFireDB -n 1 -a 127.0.0.1:11001 -d ./data ./bin/IceFireDB -n 2 -a 127.0.0.1:11002 -d ./data -j 127.0.0.1:11001 ./bin/IceFireDB -n 3 -a 127.0.0.1:11003 -d ./data -j 127.0.0.1:11001 When joining, the node dials the address with AUTH (if --auth/ICEFIREDB_AUTH is set) and TLS (if a certificate is configured), asks for the current cluster state, adds itself, and then catches up from the log. A node restarted on the same data directory does not need -j again — it rejoins from its persisted Raft state.
Use --advertise whenever the bind address is not the address peers should dial (containers, NAT, multiple interfaces):
./bin/IceFireDB -n 2 -a 0.0.0.0:11001 --advertise 10.0.0.12:11001 -d /var/lib/icefiredb -j 10.0.0.11:11001 The advertised address is what clients receive in -MOVED redirects and what other nodes add to the Raft configuration, so it must be reachable by peers and by clients.
Consistency model # Operation Where it runs Guarantee Write command (SET, HSET, RPUSH, …) Leader only, through the Raft log Applied in the same order on every node; a write is acknowledged after quorum commit Read command, no --openreads Node that receives it; on a follower it is refused Followers answer -MOVED 0 <leader>; the client retries against the leader Read command, --openreads Any node May return stale data (whatever the local log has applied) RAFT …, CLUSTER …, MACHINE, BARRIER Receiving node Administrative, not replicated With --try-errors the redirect error becomes -TRY <leader> and the CLUSTER command is disabled; this exists for clients that need to distinguish “retry elsewhere” from “the cluster moved me”.
Follower reads are only served once the node considers the log reasonably loaded; until then it answers as a non-leader.
Topology management # Membership changes go through the Raft configuration, not a config file. The two supported paths are equivalent — the first is what -j does internally:
# path 1 — let the node add itself ./bin/IceFireDB -n 4 -a 127.0.0.1:11004 -d ./data -j 127.0.0.1:11001 # path 2 — add it from an existing node, then start it redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SERVER ADD 4 127.0.0.1:11004 redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SERVER LIST redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SERVER REMOVE 4 Rules that matter:
Add before removing when replacing a node. Removing a member shrinks the quorum requirement, and a two-node cluster has no redundancy at all — during a replacement the surviving quorum must stay large enough to elect. Never reuse a node ID with a different data directory. The ID is the Raft server ID; the state in <dir>/IceFireDB/<id>/ belongs to it. A majority must be alive to elect a leader. Losing quorum does not corrupt data, but writes stop and reads that need leadership fail with -CLUSTERDOWN. The full channel list is in System commands. Snapshots # Raft takes snapshots of the state machine so the log can be truncated. Each snapshot is written under <data-dir>/IceFireDB/<node-id>/snapshots/<snapshot-id>/state.bin. The file is a gzip-compressed stream: a 32-byte header (SNAP0001 + machine start time, timestamp, RNG seed), then every key/value pair written by writeSnapshot in snapshot.go using sds framing — one pair per entry, backend agnostic.
redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SNAPSHOT NOW # take one immediately redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SNAPSHOT LIST # id, timestamp and size per snapshot redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SNAPSHOT FILE <id> # path on the server that produced it Snapshot files are the unit of backup and disaster recovery; see Operations.
Failure behaviour # Failure Effect One follower down (3-node cluster) No impact on writes or leader stability Leader down Followers elect a new leader; in-flight uncommitted writes may be lost; clients see -MOVED/-TRY until they rediscover the leader Minority partition The minority side cannot elect, its writes fail with -CLUSTERDOWN; the majority keeps serving Node restarted with the same data dir Rejoins from persisted state, catches up from the log or a snapshot Node started with a fresh data dir but an existing node ID Rejected by the cluster as an ID conflict — clear the directory or use a new ID Reads on a follower with --openreads keep working during a leader election, at the cost of serving state that may be behind.
What clustering does not do # No sharding: every node holds the full dataset. CLUSTER SLOTS reports the whole 0-16383 range on the leader for redis-cluster-aware clients, but there is no key distribution. No read-repair or anti-entropy beyond Raft: a node that is caught up stays caught up through the log. ZINCRBY, ZREMRANGEBYRANK and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE are registered as read commands, so they do not replicate. See Compatibility.

title: Hashes
content:
Hashes # 19 commands. The hash keyspace is independent from the string keyspace at the same key name.
Cmd RW Syntax Returns Example → reply HSET W HSET KEY FIELD VALUE [FIELD VALUE ...] integer fields added HSET user:1 name ada age 36 → 2 HSETNX W HSETNX KEY FIELD VALUE integer 1 written, 0 field exists HSETNX user:1 name ada → 0 HGET R HGET KEY FIELD bulk, null if the field is absent HGET user:1 name → ada HMGET R HMGET KEY FIELD [FIELD ...] array of bulk/null HMGET user:1 name x → [ada, null] HMSET W HMSET KEY FIELD VALUE [FIELD VALUE ...] +OK HMSET user:2 name bob → OK HDEL W HDEL KEY FIELD [FIELD ...] integer fields removed HDEL user:1 age → 1 HEXISTS R HEXISTS KEY FIELD integer 0/1 HEXISTS user:1 name → 1 HGETALL R HGETALL KEY array field/value pairs HGETALL user:1 → [name, ada] HKEYS R HKEYS KEY array of fields HKEYS user:1 → [name] HVALS R HVALS KEY array of values HVALS user:1 → [ada] HLEN R HLEN KEY integer field count HLEN user:1 → 1 HSTRLEN R HSTRLEN KEY FIELD integer value length, 0 if absent HSTRLEN user:1 name → 3 HINCRBY W HINCRBY KEY FIELD increment integer new value HINCRBY stats hits 1 → 1 HKEYEXISTS R HKEYEXISTS KEY integer 0/1 — does the hash exist HKEYEXISTS user:1 → 1 HCLEAR W HCLEAR KEY integer fields removed HCLEAR user:1 → 2 HMCLEAR W HMCLEAR KEY [KEY ...] integer hashes removed HMCLEAR a b → 2 HEXPIRE W HEXPIRE KEY seconds integer 1 set, 0 key absent HEXPIRE user:1 300 → 1 HEXPIREAT W HEXPIREAT KEY unixTime integer 1/0 HEXPIREAT user:1 1767225600 → 1 HTTL R HTTL KEY integer seconds left, -1 none HTTL user:1 → 299 Notes # HCLEAR / HMCLEAR delete the whole hash (like DEL for this type) and take its expiration with it; HDEL removes individual fields. There is no HPERSIST — the handler exists but is not registered. HSET counts only newly created fields; overwriting an existing field counts 0. HGETALL answers field/value pairs in the storage’s iteration order. Do not rely on it for ordering — sort client-side if it matters. HGET of a field whose value is empty answers an empty bulk string on the local backends and null on the decentralized ones — the two states are not distinguishable there. See Compatibility. HSTRLEN reports 0 both for a missing field and for an empty one. Expiry: HEXPIRE/HEXPIREAT/HTTL act on the hash, independently of any string at the same key.

title: Protocol
content:
Protocol layer # The engine speaks RESP — the Redis serialization protocol — so any Redis client works without a shim. This page covers what the protocol layer does beyond parsing bytes.
One socket, two protocols # There is exactly one TCP listener (tcp4, address from -a). On it arrive:
Client connections: RESP from applications. Peer connections: the Raft transport between nodes. They are told apart by a sniffing listener: a peer opens the connection by writing a fixed magic marker followed by the cluster auth token (transportMarker in vendor/github.com/tidwall/uhaha), and anything that does not start with that marker is treated as a RESP client. This is why TLS, the port and --advertise are shared between data and replication traffic — and why --advertise must name the address peers can reach.
Request handling # Step Behaviour Parsing RESP arrays, plus inline (telnet-style) commands Command name Lowercased before dispatch — commands are case-insensitive Pipelining Supported: requests are executed in order, replies are written in order Connection state Only AUTH state per connection; no per-connection database, no SELECT Built-ins PING, ECHO, QUIT, AUTH, SHUTDOWN are answered by the server before dispatch Everything else Dispatched to the command table (110 data commands + RAFT/CLUSTER/MACHINE/BARRIER/VERSION) Unknown commands answer ERR unknown command '<name>'.
Reply mapping # Handlers return Go values; the RESP writer maps them mechanically:
Go value RESP nil null bulk $-1 []byte / string bulk string $n [][]byte / []string / []interface{} array *n redcon.SimpleString simple string +… redcon.SimpleInt, int64, int integer :n error error -… Values are never returned as simple strings: a simple string cannot carry \r\n, and a value with a CRLF in it would corrupt the stream.
Cluster semantics on the wire # Situation Reply Write or leader-only read sent to a follower -MOVED 0 <advertised-addr> Same, with --try-errors -TRY <advertised-addr> No leader (no quorum) -CLUSTERDOWN … Cluster-aware client asks for topology CLUSTER SLOTS → one range 0-16383 on the leader; CLUSTER NODES/INFO The MOVED slot is always 0: there is no sharding, so every key “belongs” to the single master. A client that follows MOVED redirects ends up on the leader, which is exactly the intended behaviour.
Errors # All errors are RESP errors, and they use Redis’ prefixes where a client library looks for them:
Prefix Meaning -ERR … Bad arguments, bad syntax, failed validation -MOVED … / -TRY … Redirect to the leader -CLUSTERDOWN … No leader / no quorum -unauthorized AUTH missing or wrong -ERR invalid key size / invalid value size ledis limits: key ≤ 1024 B, value ≤ 1 GiB WRONGTYPE is never produced — see Compatibility.
Not in the protocol layer # No MULTI/EXEC, no SUBSCRIBE, no WATCH, no inline SELECT. Pub/sub lives in a different binary ( IceFireDB-PubSub).

title: Benchmarking
content:
Benchmarking # This page describes how to measure the engine. It deliberately contains no performance numbers: a number without the commit, hardware, backend and flags that produced it is noise.
Load generators that work # redis-benchmark and memtier_benchmark both work, because the wire protocol is RESP.
# baseline: one connection per request, no pipeline redis-benchmark -h 127.0.0.1 -p 11001 -t set,get -n 200000 -c 50 # pipelined redis-benchmark -h 127.0.0.1 -p 11001 -t set,get -n 1000000 -c 50 -P 16 # mixed, with memtier memtier_benchmark -s 127.0.0.1 -p 11001 --protocol=redis \ --clients=50 --threads=4 --ratio=1:1 --test-time=120 --key-pattern=S:S What they will not exercise:
Not covered Why SCAN/XSCAN pagination No built-in workload; drive it from a script Cluster redirects Benchmark against the leader, or expect -MOVED in the error count TTL expiry pressure Add EX to the SET payload and watch INFO Store Raft apply latency The write is acknowledged after quorum; add nodes to see the delta What to hold constant # Record all of these with any result, or the number is not comparable:
Commit — git rev-parse HEAD, and the BuildVersion from -h. Backend — --storage-backend, and for badger/hybriddb the host’s RAM (the drivers open with 1 GB memtable/large caches by default). Durability — --nosync on or off. This is usually the single largest factor on writes. Cluster size and read mode — 1 node vs 3 nodes; --openreads vs leader-only. Client side — connection count, pipeline depth, value size, and whether the client is on the same host (loopback hides the network). Workloads worth running # Workload Command shape What it tells you Point write SET key <256B> Raft + storage write path Point read GET key Cache + storage read path Counter INCR hits Read-modify-write inside the apply loop Hash write HSET k f v Multi-record encoding cost List push/pop RPUSH q v / LPOP q Index encoding, meta updates ZSet write ZADD board <score> m Two indexes per member Range read ZRANGE board 0 100 WITHSCORES Index scan efficiency Fat value SET k <64KiB> Allocation, reply size, GC pressure Reading the server side while you load it # watch -n1 'redis-cli -p 11001 INFO | sed -n "/# Store/,/# Mem/p"' curl -s http://127.0.0.1:11002/metrics | grep icefiredb_connected_clients INFO gives per-process counters (get, get_missing, put, batch_commit, and their total times), which is usually more informative than the load generator’s own percentiles: a rising batch_commit_total_time with flat throughput means the storage device, not the engine, is the limit.
Anti-patterns # Benchmarking a follower without --openreads. Every read becomes a redirect and the number measures your client’s retry loop. Comparing --nosync runs against durable ones. Different guarantees; report both or neither. Using LINSERT/LREM in a throughput test. They rebuild the whole list; they measure O(n) rewrites, not list performance. Ignoring the apply loop. Throughput is bounded by one apply goroutine, so more client threads stop helping at some point; find that point instead of assuming it away. Quoting numbers from this page. There are none, on purpose.

title: Lists
content:
Lists # 18 commands. Lists are stored as an indexed sequence; two of these commands rebuild the whole list.
Cmd RW Syntax Returns Example → reply LPUSH W LPUSH KEY VALUE [VALUE ...] integer new length LPUSH q a b → 2 RPUSH W RPUSH KEY VALUE [VALUE ...] integer new length RPUSH q c → 3 LPOP W LPOP KEY bulk head element, null if empty LPOP q → b RPOP W RPOP KEY bulk tail element, null if empty RPOP q → c LLEN R LLEN KEY integer element count LLEN q → 1 LINDEX R LINDEX KEY index bulk, null if out of range LINDEX q 0 → a LRANGE R LRANGE KEY start stop array (inclusive, negative offsets from the end) LRANGE q 0 -1 → [a] LSET W LSET KEY index VALUE +OK LSET q 0 z → OK LTRIM W LTRIM KEY start stop +OK LTRIM q 0 0 → OK RPOPLPUSH W RPOPLPUSH source destination bulk moved element, null if source empty RPOPLPUSH q backup → z LINSERT W LINSERT KEY BEFORE|AFTER pivot VALUE integer new length; 0 pivot absent; -1 key absent LINSERT q BEFORE z y → 2 LREM W LREM KEY count VALUE integer elements removed LREM q 0 z → 1 LKEYEXISTS R LKEYEXISTS KEY integer 0/1 — does the list exist LKEYEXISTS q → 1 LCLEAR W LCLEAR KEY integer elements removed LCLEAR q → 1 LMCLEAR W LMCLEAR KEY [KEY ...] integer lists removed LMCLEAR a b → 2 LEXPIRE W LEXPIRE KEY seconds integer 1/0 LEXPIRE q 600 → 1 LEXPIREAT W LEXPIREAT KEY unixTime integer 1/0 LEXPIREAT q 1767225600 → 1 LTTL R LTTL KEY integer seconds left, -1 none LTTL q → 599 Notes # LPUSH q a b produces [b, a] — each element is pushed to the head in turn, as in Redis. LREM KEY count VALUE: count > 0 removes from the head, count < 0 from the tail, count = 0 every occurrence. LINSERT and LREM are O(n) and are not transactional. The storage layer has no primitive for them, so the handler reads the list, clears it, and rewrites it (restoring the TTL). It happens inside one Raft apply, so no other client observes a partial list, but a backend failure mid-rebuild leaves the list truncated. Do not use them on long lists in a hot path — prefer LTRIM or bounded queues. There is no LPERSIST: the handler is not registered. LCLEAR/LMCLEAR delete the list and its TTL. No blocking commands. BLPOP/BRPOP are deliberately not registered: a blocking read inside the Raft apply loop either stalls the log or consumes the queue without a rollback path. LRANGE with start > stop answers an empty array; negative indexes count from the tail.

title: Network
content:
Network layer # Two independent networks exist, and they solve different problems. Confusing them is the most common architectural mistake when reading about IceFireDB.
Intra-site network Inter-site network Purpose One consistent copy of the data Replicate across sites / regions Technology Raft (hashicorp/raft) libp2p + pubsub (crdt, ipfs-log, ipfs-synckv drivers) Topology Leader + voters, quorum required Peer-to-peer, no leader, eventual Configured by -a, -j, --advertise, --raft-backend, --auth, TLS --servicename, --nettopic, --datatopic Enabled by Always Only with a P2P storage backend A common deployment runs a Raft cluster per site (strong consistency inside), with one node per site using a P2P backend to exchange data between sites (eventual consistency across). The engine does not combine the two for you — they are separate layers, and the P2P layer is a property of the driver, not of the server.
Intra-site: Raft # Each node listens on exactly one socket. Peer connections identify themselves with a transport marker plus the auth token, so replication traffic and client traffic share the port and the TLS certificate. The Raft log and stable store live in <data-dir>/IceFireDB/<node-id>/store/, in leveldb (default) or bolt (--raft-backend). --advertise sets the address other nodes store for this node. Without it, the bound address is used, which is wrong behind NAT or in containers. Joining: -j <addr> (the node adds itself) or RAFT SERVER ADD id address from the leader. Snapshots: taken by the Raft layer, written to snapshots/<id>/state.bin via writeSnapshot; the log is truncated behind them. Clock: Raft drives the machine clock through the internal replicated TICK command (default every 200 ms) so that time-dependent commands agree across replicas. --localtime replaces the remote time source with the local one, which is faster and riskier. Inter-site: P2P drivers # The crdt, ipfs-log and ipfs-synckv drivers open a libp2p host as part of the storage layer:
Driver Discovery / transport Data model Identity crdt libp2p DHT + pubsub, namespaced icefiredb-crdt-kv CRDT map over a local Badger/LevelDB --servicename + --nettopic ipfs-log IPFS pubsub + icefiredb-ipfs-log Append-only operation log, merged per peer --ipfs-log-dbname ipfs-synckv IPFS node + ipfs-log, optional AES-256 Versioned KV, IPFS as source of truth, local mirror --ipfs-synckv-key for encryption Operational consequences:
All three flags must match across the nodes that should see each other. --servicename, --nettopic and --datatopic are the rendezvous: a mismatch silently creates two independent networks rather than an error. No quorum, no leader. Writes succeed locally and propagate when peers connect; a partitioned peer keeps accepting writes and merges on rejoin (CRDT semantics), which is a very different contract from the Raft layer above. IPFS must be reachable at --ipfs-endpoint (http://localhost:5001, the API port) for ipfs, ipfs-synckv and ipfs-log. A gateway on :8080 is not an API endpoint. Peers are trusted at the network level. The mesh relies on the shared discovery names; there is no per-peer authorization. See Security. Ports in a typical deployment # Port Protocol Purpose 11001 RESP / TLS Clients and Raft peers (single socket) 11002 HTTP /healthz, /readyz, /metrics (--metrics) 26063 HTTP pprof (--pprof) 5001 HTTP API IPFS daemon, reachable from the node (not exposed by it) random libp2p P2P driver connections, egress + ephemeral inbound What the network layer does not do # No service mesh integration, no gossip-based membership beyond libp2p discovery. No cross-site consistency guarantee: the P2P layer is eventual, the Raft layer is per-cluster. No multi-cluster federation: two Raft clusters do not merge automatically.

title: Storage backends
content:
Storage backends # --storage-backend <name> selects the driver that sits under the ledis data model. The command layer is written against store.driver.IDB, so the same commands run on every backend — what changes is where the bytes live, who replicates them, and how much you can trust the driver.
type IDB interface { Close() error Get(key []byte) ([]byte, error) Put(key []byte, value []byte) error Delete(key []byte) error SyncPut(key []byte, value []byte) error SyncDelete(key []byte) error NewIterator() IIterator NewWriteBatch() IWriteBatch NewSnapshot() (ISnapshot, error) Compact() error GetStorageEngine() interface{} } What each backend is # --storage-backend Where data lives Replication External dependency goleveldb (default) Local LevelDB (pure Go) Raft only — badger Local BadgerDB v4, ZSTD compression Raft only — hybriddb Local LevelDB + Ristretto hot cache, per-driver metrics Raft only — oss S3-compatible object store, local LevelDB index + Ristretto cache Raft only S3/MinIO endpoint ipfs Local LevelDB whose values are fetched from IPFS by CID Raft only IPFS API (not a gateway) ipfs-synckv IPFS as source of truth + local mirror + version metadata, optional AES-256 IPFS/ipfs-log P2P IPFS API + P2P crdt Local Badger + icefiredb-crdt-kv over libp2p pubsub P2P CRDT libp2p peers ipfs-log Append-only icefiredb-ipfs-log store over IPFS pubsub P2P log IPFS + P2P leveldb (the cgo driver) and orbitdb are not compiled into the binary: the former is never imported, the latter is commented out in main.go/flags.go. Passing either name fails at startup with “unknown driver”.
Choosing one # Default / most workloads — goleveldb. Pure Go, no cgo, predictable memory, no external services. Write-heavy local workloads — badger. Note the driver opens with large fixed defaults (1 GB memtable, 1 GB block cache, 100 goroutines/compactors), so size the host accordingly. Read-heavy working sets that fit in RAM — hybriddb. The hot tier absorbs reads, and the driver registers read_operations, write_operations, bytes_read, errors … into INFO. Data that must outlive the host — oss, with --oss-endpoint, --oss-ak, --oss-sk. Every write goes to the object store and a local LevelDB index keeps it addressable; keep the local disk because it carries the index. Multi-site / decentralized — ipfs-synckv or crdt. Both replicate through libp2p pubsub and are configured with --servicename, --nettopic, --datatopic (all three must match across nodes). Not as a general backend today — ipfs. Its write path stores the raw value locally while the read path treats the stored bytes as an IPFS CID and cats them, so a value written through the engine does not round-trip. Use ipfs-synckv when you want IPFS persistence. Per-backend configuration # Backend Flags Defaults ipfs, ipfs-synckv --ipfs-endpoint http://localhost:5001 (the API port, not the 8080 gateway) ipfs-synckv --ipfs-synckv-key empty → no encryption; a 32-byte key enables AES-256 ipfs-log --ipfs-log-dbname, or env IPFS_LOG_DBNAME ifdb-event-kv-ipfs-log oss --oss-endpoint, --oss-ak, --oss-sk http://localhost:9000 + placeholder credentials crdt, ipfs-log --servicename, --nettopic, --datatopic icefiredb, icefiredb-net, icefiredb-data The hot-cache capacity of oss, ipfs and ipfs-synckv is not configurable from the command line: it is the driver constant of 1024 MB. See Configuration.
Guarantees you do and do not get # You get
The same command semantics on every backend, including the per-type keyspaces and per-type expiry. Raft snapshot/restore that is backend-agnostic: writeSnapshot iterates the driver’s snapshot and streams key/value pairs in sds format inside a gzip file, so a backup taken on badger can be restored into a fresh goleveldb node (see Operations). Backend metrics in INFO for hybriddb, ipfs, ipfs-synckv, oss. You do not get
No cross-backend on-disk compatibility. Do not change --storage-backend for an existing data directory; the formats are unrelated. No “empty value” distinction on the decentralized drivers. They collapse “missing” and “empty”, so an empty string reads back as a nil reply. Pinned in Compatibility. No driver-level retry or repair. A failed write surfaces as a command error; on a P2P driver a temporarily unreachable peer shows up as missing data until the log catches up. Test coverage, by driver # Driver Tests Notes goleveldb engine-level compat suite (DRIVER=goleveldb make test-compat) via ledisdb badger driver/badger/db_test.go + engine suite (default DRIVER=badger) — hybriddb driver/hybriddb/{db,iterator,snapshot,write_batch}_test.go — ipfs-synckv driver/ipfs-synckv/{db,iterator,singularity}_test.go needs an IPFS daemon oss driver/oss/s3_test.go needs S3/MinIO (CI runs localstack) ipfs, crdt, ipfs-log no unit tests in this repository exercised manually against real peers That table is the honest version of “supported”: a driver with no test can still work, but nothing in CI will tell you when it stops working.

title: Ecosystem
content:
Ecosystem libraries and components # The engine is one piece. These are the libraries and services around it, all in the same GitHub organisation.
Libraries used by the storage drivers # Project Used by What it does icefiredb-crdt-kv driver/crdt CRDT key/value store over libp2p pubsub; merges concurrent writes without coordination icefiredb-ipfs-log driver/ipfs-log, driver/ipfs-synckv Immutable, operation-based append-only log for distributed systems, stored in IPFS and merged through pubsub IceFireDB/uhaha (fork) the binary Raft application framework: RESP server, log, snapshots, RAFT/CLUSTER commands IceFireDB/ledisdb (fork) the binary The data model: per-type keyspaces, TTLs, encodings Two of these are forked and pinned in go.mod via replace directives. Vendor updates to them are behavioural changes to the engine, so go mod vendor diffs deserve a real review.
Services in this repository # IceFireDB-PubSub # Redis PubSub protocol over a libp2p network. Clients keep using SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH; the server propagates messages across peers, including peers behind NAT.
cd IceFireDB-PubSub make ./bin/IceFireDB-PubSub -c ./config/config.yaml # proxy.local_port: 16379 redis-cli -p 16379 SUBSCRIBE name redis-cli -p 16379 PUBLISH name hello Configuration is config/config.yaml: proxy.local_port, p2p.* (discovery id, command topic, mode, host ip/port), pprof_debug, log.level, ip_white_list, cache, ignore_cmd. See IceFireDB-PubSub.
IceFireDB-SQLite # MySQL protocol in front of a SQLite file, with statements propagated to peers so every node can answer SQL locally.
cd IceFireDB-SQLite make ./bin/IceFireDB-SQLite -c ./config/config.yaml # server.addr: ":23306" mysql -h 127.0.0.1 -P 23306 -u root -p # password from config userlist IceFireDB-SQLProxy # MySQL protocol proxy that replays statements to a MySQL backend, with separate admin/readonly connection pools and per-tenant users.
cd IceFireDB-SQLProxy make ./bin/IceFireDB-SQLProxy -c ./config/config.yaml # server.addr: ":33306" IceFireDB-Redis-Proxy # RESP proxy that replicates commands to a single-node or clustered Redis, with optional read/write separation and caching.
cd IceFireDB-Redis-Proxy make ./bin/IceFireDB-Redis-Proxy -c ./config/config.yaml # proxy.local_port: 16379 redhub # A multi-threaded RESP server framework (epoll/raw-epoll based) used by the proxies; useful on its own when you need a fast Redis-protocol front end without the database.
Which one do I need? # Goal Component Redis-compatible KV with Raft and pluggable storage NoSQL engine (this docs section) Decentralized pub/sub between services IceFireDB-PubSub SQL semantics on each node, replicated IceFireDB-SQLite Existing MySQL/Redis made multi-site without rewriting the app SQLProxy / Redis-Proxy Build a RESP front end redhub Not implemented, despite older documentation # OrbitDB driver — disabled in main.go/flags.go (driver/orbitdb is not built). NATS integration, vector/AI search, GraphQL endpoint — no code in this tree. IceFireDB-Proxy as a standalone RESP cluster proxy — the repository ships IceFireDB-Redis-Proxy instead.

title: Security
content:
Security # The engine has three security-relevant surfaces: the RESP listener, the Raft transport, and the optional admin HTTP servers. They share one credential and one certificate.
Transport encryption (TLS) # ./bin/IceFireDB --tls-cert ./server.crt --tls-key ./server.key -a 0.0.0.0:11001 -d /var/lib/icefiredb Both flags are required together — providing one without the other is a startup error. TLS is applied to the single listening socket. RESP clients and the Raft transport both arrive on it, and the server decides which is which by sniffing the first bytes. There is no second port. The value of --advertise must therefore be the TLS address peers and clients use. Clients must speak TLS too: redis-cli --tls --cacert ./ca.crt -h host -p 11001, or the equivalent client option (go-redis: TLSConfig, Python redis.Redis(ssl=True), Node tls: {}). The certificate needs a DNS: SAN for the name clients use; the server copies the first DNS SAN into its tls.Config.ServerName for outbound connections. No client certificates. tls.Config is built with Certificates only, so there is no mTLS and no client identity. Peers authenticate with the shared token, not a certificate. Cluster authorization # export ICEFIREDB_AUTH='openssl rand -hex 32' # preferred: not visible in the process list ./bin/IceFireDB -a 0.0.0.0:11001 -d /var/lib/icefiredb # or ./bin/IceFireDB --auth '<token>' -a 0.0.0.0:11001 -d /var/lib/icefiredb What it does:
A client must send AUTH <token> before any other command. A wrong token answers -unauthorized. So the first command on a connection has to be AUTH. Every mainstream client library does this automatically when you configure a password (redis-cli -a, go-redis Password, Python password=, Node password:); a hand-rolled client that sends a command first will not get a clean error reply in the current build (see Known gaps). Nodes use the same token to authenticate to each other when joining a cluster, reading the log index, and transferring leadership. Every node must share the token, and changing it on one node breaks the cluster. It is a single shared secret with no notion of users, roles or per-command permissions. There is no ACL subsystem in this engine today: whoever holds the token can write, flush (FLUSHALL), change cluster membership (RAFT SERVER ADD|REMOVE) and shut the process down (SHUTDOWN). What it does not do:
No rate limiting, no lockout, no token rotation, no per-key authorization. No audit log of who ran what (the MONITOR-style observer is internal and does not expose raft/auth/cluster commands). It does not encrypt traffic — pair it with --tls-cert/--tls-key on any network you do not own. Admin HTTP servers # Endpoint group Flag Default bind Auth /healthz, /readyz, /metrics --metrics 127.0.0.1:11002 none pprof (/debug/pprof/*) --pprof 127.0.0.1:26063 none Both are off by default and bound to loopback precisely because they carry no authentication. /metrics and /debug/pprof leak operational detail and block or allocate memory under load; keep them on a private interface, a sidecar, or behind a reverse proxy that enforces identity.
Recommended baseline # ICEFIREDB_AUTH="$(cat /run/secrets/icefiredb-auth)" \ ./bin/IceFireDB \ --tls-cert /etc/icefiredb/tls/server.crt --tls-key /etc/icefiredb/tls/server.key \ -a 0.0.0.0:11001 --advertise db1.internal:11001 \ -d /var/lib/icefiredb \ --metrics --metrics-addr 127.0.0.1:11002 \ --storage-backend goleveldb Never expose the RESP port without TLS unless it is only reachable over a private network. Keep the token in ICEFIREDB_AUTH or a .env file (the binary loads godotenv at startup), never in a shell history or a unit file that is world-readable. Leave --metrics/--pprof on loopback; scrape them from the same host. Treat FLUSHALL, RAFT SERVER REMOVE and SHUTDOWN as root-equivalent operations, because they are. Run the process as an unprivileged user that owns the data directory; -d needs write access only to that tree. Toolchain and known vulnerabilities # The dependency set is checked two ways: GitHub Dependabot alerts (anything touching a module in go.mod) and govulncheck . (only vulnerabilities reachable from the code that is actually built). Only the second describes risk, and the current accepted set is two entries, both on the libp2p path:
ID Module Why it is not fixed When it is reachable GO-2026-4479 github.com/pion/dtls/v2@v2.2.12 No fixed v2 release exists; kubo, boxo, ipfs-lite and the IceFireDB forks all still require it libp2p WebRTC transport, i.e. only with a decentralized backend (crdt, ipfs, ipfs-log, ipfs-synckv) GO-2024-3218 github.com/libp2p/go-libp2p-kad-dht@v0.38.0 The fix needs kad-dht >= 0.40, which changed dht.New/dualdht.New signatures and breaks the same upstream set Same libp2p/DHT path Practically: the GA backends (goleveldb, hybriddb) never enter that code at runtime, and the mitigation is network exposure — keep the libp2p port of a decentralized backend off untrusted networks. The full record, with the condition under which each entry can be closed, is in the engine’s SECURITY.md; re-check with govulncheck . after any coordinated upgrade of kubo, ipfs-lite and the IceFireDB forks.
Known gaps # No per-user ACLs (tracked as future work, not implemented in this tree). No token rotation protocol: rotating the token means a coordinated restart. No protection against a malicious peer that already holds the token — cluster membership is trust-on-first-use plus the shared secret. A command sent before AUTH (or after a failed AUTH) is not answered with an error reply in the current build: the dispatcher leaves the response slot empty for unauthenticated commands. Send AUTH first, as every client library does, and treat the token as a connect-time credential rather than something you can prompt for mid-connection.

title: Sets
content:
Sets # 21 commands: membership, the three set-algebra families, expiry, and deterministic SPOP.
Cmd RW Syntax Returns Example → reply SADD W SADD KEY MEMBER [MEMBER ...] integer members added SADD tags go db → 2 SREM W SREM KEY MEMBER [MEMBER ...] integer members removed SREM tags db → 1 SCARD R SCARD KEY integer cardinality SCARD tags → 1 SISMEMBER R SISMEMBER KEY MEMBER integer 0/1 SISMEMBER tags go → 1 SMEMBERS R SMEMBERS KEY array of members SMEMBERS tags → [go] SDIFF R SDIFF KEY [KEY ...] array members in the first but no later set SDIFF a b → [x] SDIFFSTORE W SDIFFSTORE dest KEY [KEY ...] integer size of the result SDIFFSTORE out a b → 1 SINTER R SINTER KEY [KEY ...] array members in every set SINTER a b → [y] SINTERSTORE W SINTERSTORE dest KEY [KEY ...] integer size of the result SINTERSTORE out a b → 1 SUNION R SUNION KEY [KEY ...] array members in any set SUNION a b → [x,y] SUNIONSTORE W SUNIONSTORE dest KEY [KEY ...] integer size of the result SUNIONSTORE out a b → 2 SMOVE W SMOVE source destination MEMBER integer 1 moved, 0 not a member SMOVE a b x → 1 SPOP W SPOP KEY [count] bare: bulk member; with count: array SPOP queue:ready → job:7 SRANDMEMBER R SRANDMEMBER KEY [count] bare: bulk; positive count: distinct array; negative: array with repeats SRANDMEMBER tags 1 → [go] SKEYEXISTS R SKEYEXISTS KEY integer 0/1 — does the set exist SKEYEXISTS tags → 1 SCLEAR W SCLEAR KEY integer members removed SCLEAR tags → 1 SMCLEAR W SMCLEAR KEY [KEY ...] integer sets removed SMCLEAR a b → 2 SEXPIRE W SEXPIRE KEY seconds integer 1/0 SEXPIRE tags 60 → 1 SEXPIREAT W SEXPIREAT KEY unixTime integer 1/0 SEXPIREAT tags 1767225600 → 1 STTL R STTL KEY integer seconds left, -1 none STTL tags → 59 SPERSIST W SPERSIST KEY integer 1 removed, 0 none SPERSIST tags → 1 Notes # SPOP is deterministic across replicas. Because it is a write command, its result must be identical on every node, so the picked member is derived from the Raft-seeded state rather than math/rand. With count, the count is clamped to the set size; count = 0 answers an empty array and a negative count is an error. SRANDMEMBER is a read command and may use real randomness (count distinct members when positive, repeats when negative). |count| is capped at 1048576. SMOVE to the same key is a no-op that returns 1 and keeps the TTL. SCLEAR/SMCLEAR delete whole sets and their expiration; SREM removes members. SPERSIST is the only *PERSIST command in the engine, and it is known to leave the expiration in place on the ipfs backend. Strings, hashes and lists have no PERSIST at all. Set algebra commands read the sets named in the arguments; *STORE variants overwrite the destination and return the size of the result.

title: Storage
content:
Storage layer # Under the command handlers sits ledis: a data model that turns five Redis types into key/value operations over a single driver.IDB. It is the reason the same commands work on a local LevelDB file and on IPFS.
Per-type keyspaces # ledis does not store “a key with a type”. It stores separate physical keys per type, each prefixed with a type byte:
Type Prefix bytes Physical keys per logical key String KVType the value Hash HashType, HSizeType one entry per field + a size counter List ListType, LMetaType one entry per index + a meta record (head/tail/size) Set SetType, SSizeType one entry per member + a size counter Sorted set ZSetType, ZSizeType, ZScoreType one entry per member + size counter + one index entry per (score, member) Expirations are separate records too (ExpMetaType, ExpTimeType), which is why a TTL belongs to the type it was set on rather than to the key name.
Consequences you can observe from the client side:
Two types can coexist at the same name (see Compatibility). SCAN has to walk five keyspaces; its cursor carries five sub-cursors. Deleting a hash (HCLEAR) removes many physical keys; DEL removes only the string’s. Physical key encoding # Composite keys are length-prefixed and separator-delimited rather than hashed:
hash: [index][HashType][uint16 keyLen][key][':'][field] list: [index][ListType][uint16 keyLen][key][uint32 index] zset: [index][ZScoreType][uint16 keyLen][key][sep][score][member] sep for sorted sets is one of two bytes depending on the score’s sign, so the byte order of the index matches numeric score order — that is what makes ZRANGEBYSCORE a range scan instead of a full sort. Member entries are sorted by encoded key, so SMEMBERS/HKEYS order is storage order, not insertion order.
Limits enforced here, not in the handlers # Limit Value Error Key size 1024 bytes, non-empty invalid key size Hash field size 1024 bytes, non-empty invalid hash field size Set member size 1024 bytes invalid set member size Sorted-set member size 1024 bytes invalid zset member size Value size 1 GiB invalid value size Expiry timestamp in the past — invalid expire value These come from vendor/github.com/ledisdb/ledisdb/ledis/const.go; changing them means changing ledis. Note that they are much tighter than Redis’ 512 MB values and effectively unlimited keys — a 1 KiB key budget is the constraint most applications hit first.
Expiry # Expirations are stored in whole seconds and keyed per type. Timestamps are computed from the Raft clock by the handler and validated by ledis against the local clock; a timestamp <= now is rejected. Expired keys are reaped lazily/asynchronously, so a logically expired key can still be observed by an existence check on another replica. See Compatibility. TTL/HTTL/LTTL/STTL subtract the local clock from the stored timestamp and return -1 both for “no expiry” and “already expired”. Backends and durability # The driver contract is deliberately small (see Storage backends). Above it:
Writes go through ledis and then the driver’s Put/WriteBatch; --nosync disables the per-write disk sync in the Raft log layer, not in the driver. Compaction is delegated to the driver (Compact()); for goleveldb/badger that is normal LSM compaction, for crdt/ipfs-log it is a no-op. Snapshots iterate the driver and stream key/value pairs in sds format inside a gzip container, so they are backend-independent — see Operations. Why the design holds together # The command layer never assumes a specific store. It asks ledis for operations (HSet, LPush, ZRangeByScore, …), and ledis maps them onto prefixed key operations. Everything that makes the engine a database — structures, ordering, expiry — lives in that mapping, so a new backend only has to be a correct ordered KV store.
The cost is at the edges: no cross-type atomicity, O(n) list rebuilds, name-based scan cursors, and the 1024-byte key budget. Those are documented as limitations rather than papered over.

title: Codec
content:
Codec layer # The “codec” in this engine is the mapping between protocol-level structures and the KV pairs ledis writes. It is not a serialization format you can choose — it is fixed by ledis and visible only through side effects such as key limits, ordering and migration.
What gets encoded # Logical operation Physical operations SET k v Put(KVType + k, v) HSET k f v Put(HashType + k + f, v), IncrBy(HSizeType + k, 1) on a new field RPUSH k v Put(ListType + k + index, v), update LMetaType + k (head, tail, count) SADD k m Put(SetType + k + m, nil), IncrBy(SSizeType + k, 1) ZADD k score m Put(ZSetType + k + m, score), Put(ZScoreType + k + score + m, nil), size counter EXPIRE k s Put(ExpTimeType + k, timestamp), Put(ExpMetaType + k, …) Deletes are the inverse: a hash field delete removes one HashType record and decrements the size counter, while HCLEAR walks them all and removes the counters and expiry records too.
Why the type byte matters # Because the type is part of the storage key, two types never collide, and no type check is needed on read: GET k simply looks up KVType + k and returns nil if it is absent, even if a hash exists under HashType + k. That is the mechanical reason there is no WRONGTYPE — and why you cannot ask a key for its type.
Ordering guarantees that fall out of the encoding # Sorted sets are ordered by the encoded score record: sign separator, then big-endian score, then member. Range queries are index scans, and equal scores sort by member. Lists are ordered by a uint32 index with a head/tail metadata record, so LPUSH and RPUSH are both O(1) and LINDEX is a direct lookup — but LINSERT/LREM rewrite the whole range. Sets and hashes have no inherent order: iteration is physical key order of the backend, which is why reply order differs between goleveldb and badger and must not be relied on. Values are opaque # The codec never interprets values. A string value is the bytes you sent; a hash field value likewise. Compression, encryption and content addressing are driver concerns (ipfs-synckv encrypts, ipfs addresses by CID, badger compresses blocks). This is why --storage-backend changes durability and privacy but never command semantics.
Migration implications # The encoding is stable across releases in this tree; changing it would break on-disk compatibility and is why the ledger of storage behaviours in COMMAND-AUDIT.md is treated as a contract. Snapshots are not encoded: writeSnapshot streams raw physical key/value pairs, so a restore depends on the same ledis encoding being present in the target binary. Back up across versions with that in mind: restore with a binary whose ledis layer matches the snapshot’s.

title: Observability
content:
Observability # There are three ways to see what a node is doing: the HTTP endpoints, the INFO command, and pprof. All three are opt-in.
HTTP endpoints # ./bin/IceFireDB --metrics --metrics-addr 127.0.0.1:11002 -d /var/lib/icefiredb Path Response Use /healthz 200 ok whenever the process is up Liveness probe /readyz 200 ready once the storage backend has initialized; 503 not ready before that Readiness probe / rollout gate /metrics Prometheus text exposition Scraping The server is a plain http.Server with a 5-second ReadHeaderTimeout; it has no authentication, so keep it on loopback or a private interface (see Security).
Metrics exposed # The registry is not the global one — it registers exactly:
Metric Type Meaning icefiredb_connected_clients gauge RESP connections currently open go_* collector Go runtime (goroutines, GC, memstats, …) process_* collector Process CPU, RSS, FDs, start time There are no Raft metrics, no per-command counters and no latency histograms. Command and storage counters live in INFO instead (below). Scrape interval and alerting should lean on up, icefiredb_connected_clients and container-level signals.
# prometheus.yml scrape_configs: - job_name: icefiredb static_configs: - targets: ["127.0.0.1:11002"] INFO # INFO takes no arguments — INFO memory is an argument error, unlike Redis. It answers one bulk string with five sections, then one section per backend that registers extra metrics.
# Server os:linux arch:amd64 process_id:1 addr:127.0.0.1:11001 http_addr: readonly:false goroutine_num:38 gomaxprocs:8 thread_num:12 cgo_call_num:0 resp_client_num:1 ledisdb_version:... # Store name:goleveldb get:0 get_missing:0 put:0 delete:0 get_total_time:0s iter:0 iter_seek:0 iter_close:0 batch_commit:0 batch_commit_total_time:0s # Mem mem_alloc:... mem_sys:... mem_heap_alloc:... mem_head_objects:... # GC gc_last_time:... gc_num:... gc_pause_total:... gc_pause_history:... Section Fields Notes Server os, arch, process_id, addr, http_addr, readonly, goroutine_num, gomaxprocs, thread_num, cgo_call_num, resp_client_num, ledisdb_version addr is the configured bind address; readonly comes from the ledis config and is always false here Store name, get, get_missing, put, delete, get_total_time, iter, iter_seek, iter_close, batch_commit, batch_commit_total_time Counters are per-process, reset on restart Mem mem_alloc, mem_sys, mem_looksups, mem_mallocs, mem_frees, mem_total, mem_heap_alloc, mem_heap_sys, mem_head_idle, mem_head_inuse, mem_head_released, mem_head_objects Human-readable sizes (1.234G) GC gc_last_time, gc_num, gc_pause_total, gc_pause_history Last five pauses Driver sections see below Only for backends that implement Metrics() Driver sections appended by main.go:
hybriddb: read_operations, write_operations, delete_operations, bytes_read, bytes_written, errors, uptime, closed. ipfs, ipfs-synckv, oss: a hybriddb cache section (the title is a copy-paste in the drivers) with Ristretto counters — used_cost, cost_added, cost_evicted, hits, misses, ratio, keys_added, keys_evicted, keys_updated, gets_kept, gets_dropped, sets_dropped, sets_rejected. INFO is a read command: it is served by the node you ask, never replicated, and a follower answers locally.
pprof # ./bin/IceFireDB --pprof --pprof-addr 127.0.0.1:26063 -d /var/lib/icefiredb go tool pprof http://127.0.0.1:26063/debug/pprof/heap Standard net/http/pprof handlers: /debug/pprof/{profile,heap,goroutine,block,mutex,trace}. Same caveat as /metrics — no auth, loopback by default.
Cluster state # Cluster and Raft state are exposed as commands rather than metrics:
redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT LEADER # advertise address of the current leader redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT INFO # raft state/term/index snapshot redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SERVER LIST # id, address, leader flag per member redis-cli -p 11001 CLUSTER INFO # cluster_state:ok/fail, cluster_known_nodes, cluster_size redis-cli -p 11001 CLUSTER NODES # redis-cluster-shaped node lines redis-cli -p 11001 MACHINE # now / uptime / boottime from the Raft clock MACHINE HUMAN returns the same values as RFC3339 timestamps and a Go duration. See System commands.
What to alert on # Signal Where Meaning /readyz non-200 HTTP probe Storage did not initialize — the node must not take traffic up{job="icefiredb"} Prometheus The node or its metrics endpoint is gone -CLUSTERDOWN, -MOVED storms Your client metrics Write path cannot find a leader; check quorum resp_client_num growth INFO Server Connection leak in the client pool get_missing / put ratio INFO Store Read misses dominating — cache hit-rate or dataset problem gc_pause_total slope INFO GC Allocation pressure, usually large replies or big pipelines

title: Sorted sets
content:
Sorted sets # 15 commands. Scores are 64-bit integers, not doubles — the one difference that changes query results, not just the wire format.
Cmd RW Syntax Returns Example → reply ZADD W ZADD KEY score MEMBER [score MEMBER ...] integer members added ZADD board 100 ada 90 bob → 2 ZINCRBY R ⚠ ZINCRBY KEY increment MEMBER bulk new score ZINCRBY board 5 ada → 105 ZREM W ZREM KEY MEMBER [MEMBER ...] integer members removed ZREM board bob → 1 ZCARD R ZCARD KEY integer cardinality ZCARD board → 1 ZCOUNT R ZCOUNT KEY min max integer members within the score range ZCOUNT board 0 200 → 1 ZSCORE R ZSCORE KEY MEMBER bulk score, null if absent ZSCORE board ada → 105 ZRANK R ZRANK KEY MEMBER integer rank (0-based), null if absent ZRANK board ada → 0 ZREVRANK R ZREVRANK KEY MEMBER integer reverse rank, null if absent ZREVRANK board ada → 0 ZRANGE R ZRANGE KEY start stop [WITHSCORES] array members (and scores) ZRANGE board 0 -1 WITHSCORES → [ada, 105] ZREVRANGE R ZREVRANGE KEY start stop [WITHSCORES] array members (and scores) ZREVRANGE board 0 0 → [ada] ZRANGEBYSCORE R ZRANGEBYSCORE KEY min max [WITHSCORES] array members (and scores) ZRANGEBYSCORE board 100 200 → [ada] ZREVRANGEBYSCORE R ZREVRANGEBYSCORE KEY max min [WITHSCORES] array members (and scores) ZREVRANGEBYSCORE board 200 100 → [ada] ZREMRANGEBYRANK R ⚠ ZREMRANGEBYRANK KEY start stop integer members removed ZREMRANGEBYRANK board 0 0 → 1 ZREMRANGEBYSCORE R ⚠ ZREMRANGEBYSCORE KEY min max integer members removed ZREMRANGEBYSCORE board 0 50 → 0 ZCLEAR W ZCLEAR KEY integer members removed ZCLEAR board → 1 Notes # ⚠ ZINCRBY, ZREMRANGEBYRANK and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE are registered as read commands even though they mutate. Locally that is harmless; in a cluster their effect is not replicated and does not survive a leader change. Until that is fixed: compute scores client-side and write them with ZADD, and remove members with ZREM. No TTL for sorted sets. There is no ZEXPIRE/ZTTL; clear and recreate the key (ZCLEAR), or keep the expiry bookkeeping in a string key. Scores parse as int64. A float score such as 1.5 is rejected; WITHSCORES returns integers. ZRANGEBYSCORE min max is inclusive on both ends; ZREVRANGEBYSCORE max min takes the arguments in reverse order, as in Redis. ZRANK/ZREVRANK answer null for a missing member, ZSCORE likewise. All range reads are ordered by score, then by member for equal scores.

title: Operations
content:
Operations # Backup, restore, upgrade and recovery for a single node or a Raft cluster. The unit of everything is the node directory: <data-dir>/IceFireDB/<node-id>/.
What is on disk # Path Contents Backed up by main.db/ The ledis store in the selected driver’s format Copying the directory store/ Raft log + stable store (leveldb or bolt) Copying the directory snapshots/<id>/state.bin Raft state-machine snapshot: gzip header (start/ts/seed) + sds key/value stream RAFT SNAPSHOT, or copying the directory state.bin is backend-agnostic: writeSnapshot walks the driver’s snapshot and writes key, value pairs into a gzip stream. That is why a snapshot taken on a badger node restores into a goleveldb node, while the main.db/ directory itself never does. Treat the file as opaque: copy it whole (or in RAFT SNAPSHOT READ windows) and hand it back with --restore — do not unzip or edit it.
Backup # Option A — snapshot the state machine (recommended, portable)
redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SNAPSHOT NOW # returns the new snapshot id redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SNAPSHOT LIST # ids and sizes redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SNAPSHOT FILE <id> # absolute path on the server # copy that file off the host: scp db1:/var/lib/icefiredb/IceFireDB/1/snapshots/<id>/state.bin ./backup-$(date +%F).sds For large or bandwidth-limited snapshots, read it in windows instead of copying the file:
redis-cli -p 11001 --raw RAFT SNAPSHOT READ <id> RANGE 0 1048576 > part-000 redis-cli -p 11001 --raw RAFT SNAPSHOT READ <id> RANGE 1048576 1048576 > part-001 Option B — copy a node directory (fastest for a full cluster)
Stop writes, or pick a follower and let it settle, then copy the whole <data-dir>/IceFireDB/<node-id>/ tree. Copying a leader under write load gives you a directory that is internally consistent as of some recent log index, but “some index” is not a point you control — for a backup you can reason about, use Option A or quiesce the node.
Restore # --restore bootstraps a brand-new single-node cluster from a snapshot file:
mkdir -p /var/lib/icefiredb-restore ./bin/IceFireDB -n 1 -a 127.0.0.1:11001 -d /var/lib/icefiredb-restore \ --restore ./backup-2026-11-08.sds Rules, all enforced by the Raft layer:
--restore is ignored if <data-dir>/IceFireDB/<node-id>/ already exists. Use a fresh directory. It cannot be combined with -j; the restored node is the new cluster of one. Every other node must be wiped and re-joined with -j <restored-node-addr> — their logs refer to a cluster history that no longer exists. Restore batches writes 1000 pairs at a time, so memory stays bounded and a large snapshot does not need to fit in RAM. Rolling upgrade # One node at a time, followers first, leader last:
Check health — CLUSTER INFO reports cluster_state:ok, RAFT SERVER LIST lists every member, /readyz is 200 on all nodes. Upgrade a follower. Stop it, replace the binary, start it with the same -n, -a and -d. It rejoins from persisted Raft state and catches up from the log or a snapshot. Wait for /readyz to return 200 and for its RAFT INFO index to catch up before touching the next node. Upgrade the leader last. Stop it; a follower is elected; start the upgraded binary; it rejoins as a follower. Never take down a majority at once: without quorum, writes fail with -CLUSTERDOWN until a leader can be elected again.
Compatibility rules for an existing data directory:
Do Don’t Keep -n, -a and -d stable Change the node ID or move the directory to another node Keep --auth/ICEFIREDB_AUTH identical on every node Rotate the token node-by-node Keep --storage-backend as it was Switch backend on an existing main.db Keep --raft-backend as it was Switch Raft log format under an existing store/ Disaster recovery # Lost one node — give it a fresh directory (or wipe the old one), then join it:
rm -rf /var/lib/icefiredb/IceFireDB/3 ./bin/IceFireDB -n 3 -a 10.0.0.13:11001 --advertise 10.0.0.13:11001 -d /var/lib/icefiredb -j 10.0.0.11:11001 If the old membership entry is still present and the node cannot rejoin, remove it first from a healthy member: RAFT SERVER REMOVE 3, then start the node with -j.
Lost quorum — writes are down but the data still exists on the surviving nodes. Restore the newest snapshot into a fresh single-node cluster (--restore, above), then re-add the other nodes with RAFT SERVER ADD or -j. Data written after that snapshot is lost; this is the only recovery that does not need a majority.
Corrupt storage — main.db/ can be repaired per driver (e.g. GoLevelDB/Badger recovery tools), but the supported path is: remove the node, restore from the latest snapshot, rejoin.
Routine checks # # is the process serving? curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:11002/healthz curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:11002/readyz # is the cluster healthy? redis-cli -p 11001 CLUSTER INFO redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SERVER LIST # is it roughly in sync? (compare a sample on two nodes) redis-cli -p 11001 --scan --pattern 'sample:*' | head -50 | xargs -n1 redis-cli -p 11001 GET Capacity notes # Every node stores the full dataset; there is no sharding. Disk sizing is per node, not per cluster. --nosync trades durability for write throughput; never use it on a node you intend to restore from after a power loss. badger opens with 1 GB memtable and 1 GB block cache defaults; budget them. Raft snapshots accumulate under snapshots/; the Raft layer prunes old ones, but on a node that is never snapshotted the log grows until the next snapshot — plan for that disk usage.

title: Scan
content:
Scan # 8 commands in two families with two different cursor contracts. Getting them mixed up is the most common integration bug with this engine.
Cmd RW Syntax Returns Example → reply SCAN R SCAN cursor [MATCH glob] [COUNT n] [TYPE type] array [cursor, keys]; cursor 0 ends the walk SCAN 0 MATCH user:* COUNT 100 → [cursor, [user:1, user:2]] HSCAN R HSCAN KEY cursor [MATCH glob] [COUNT n] array [cursor, [field, value, ...]] HSCAN user:1 0 COUNT 10 → [0, [name, ada]] SSCAN R SSCAN KEY cursor [MATCH glob] [COUNT n] array [cursor, [member, ...]] SSCAN tags 0 → [0, [go]] ZSCAN R ZSCAN KEY cursor [MATCH glob] [COUNT n] array [cursor, [member, score, ...]] ZSCAN board 0 → [0, [ada, 105]] XSCAN R XSCAN type cursor [MATCH regex] [COUNT n] [ASC|DESC] array [cursor, keys]; empty cursor ends the walk XSCAN KV "" COUNT 5 → [key:5, [...]] XHSCAN R XHSCAN KEY cursor [MATCH regex] [COUNT n] [ASC|DESC] array [cursor, [field, value, ...]] XHSCAN user:1 "" COUNT 5 → [name, [name, ada]] XSSCAN R XSSCAN KEY cursor [MATCH regex] [COUNT n] [ASC|DESC] array [cursor, [member, ...]] XSSCAN tags "" → [go, [go]] XZSCAN R XZSCAN KEY cursor [MATCH regex] [COUNT n] [ASC|DESC] array [cursor, [member, score, ...]] XZSCAN board "" → [ada, [ada, 105]] The Redis family # SCAN / HSCAN / SSCAN / ZSCAN follow Redis’ shape but not Redis’ cursor encoding.
Start at cursor 0; the walk is over when the reply’s cursor is 0. SCAN’s cursor is an opaque base64 string that carries five sub-cursors, one per keyspace (string, hash, list, set, zset). It is not a number and not a key offset. HSCAN / SSCAN / ZSCAN answer the last field or member name as the cursor. Consequences: A field literally named 0 collides with the end marker. Client helpers that parse the cursor as an integer (go-redis’ typed HScan, for example) reject it. Use the generic command API: redis-cli, Do("hscan", …), execute_command. MATCH takes a Redis glob (*, ?, [abc], \\ escape), translated to a regexp and applied by the handler over a bounded page. SCAN supports TYPE string|hash|list|set|zset; an unknown type answers an empty result. Default COUNT is 10 when omitted. The X family # XSCAN / XHSCAN / XSSCAN / XZSCAN are the engine’s native scans:
Start at an empty cursor ""; the walk is over when an empty cursor comes back. MATCH is a regular expression, not a glob, and is passed to the storage layer. ASC / DESC choose the direction (DESC walks with RevScan). XSCAN’s first argument is the type name: KV, HASH, LIST, SET, ZSET (case-insensitive; anything else is an invalid key type error). Rules that apply to both # COUNT is a hint, capped at 10000. It bounds allocation, not the number of returned items. A page can come back empty while the cursor still advances. Never stop on a short or empty page; loop until the cursor is 0 (Redis family) or "" (X family). Scans do not take a snapshot: keys added or removed during a walk may or may not appear. That is the same guarantee Redis gives. Both families are read commands, so on a follower they need --openreads (or a redirect to the leader). Loop patterns # # Redis family — go-redis's typed HScan does not work; use the generic API cursor = 0 while True: cursor, keys = r.execute_command("SCAN", cursor, "MATCH", "user:*", "COUNT", 500) for k in keys: ... if cursor == b"0" or cursor == "0": break # X family — empty cursor terminates cursor = "" while True: cursor, items = r.execute_command("XSCAN", "HASH", cursor, "MATCH", "^user:", "COUNT", 500) for k in items: ... if not cursor: break # redis-cli drives the cursor for you on SCAN redis-cli -p 11001 --scan --pattern 'user:*' | head

title: Server
content:
Server # Three commands in the data surface. Everything else an operator needs (RAFT, CLUSTER, MACHINE, BARRIER, AUTH, SHUTDOWN, VERSION) lives in System commands.
