Cmd RW Syntax Returns Example → reply INFO R INFO bulk multi-line report INFO → # Server\r\nversion… FLUSHALL W FLUSHALL integer keys removed FLUSHALL → (integer) 42 FLUSHDB W FLUSHDB integer keys removed — alias of FLUSHALL FLUSHDB → (integer) 42 INFO takes no arguments # INFO memory, INFO server and INFO replication are argument errors; the command is len(args) != 1 → wrong number of arguments. Ask for INFO and read the section you need out of the single reply. The sections and their fields are documented in Observability.
INFO is a read command: the receiving node answers from its own state, and it is never replicated.
FLUSHDB is FLUSHALL # The engine has one logical database, so FLUSHDB is implemented as an alias of FLUSHALL. Both:
are write commands, so they go through the Raft log and are replicated (that is why they return a count rather than OK); delete every key in every per-type keyspace (string, hash, list, set, zset) including their expirations; are unrecoverable — there is no undo and no soft delete. Treat them as root-equivalent operations. Not implemented # Command Status SELECT Not implemented — one database, always index 0 DBSIZE Not registered KEYS Not registered — use SCAN MULTI / EXEC / WATCH Not implemented — no transactions in the command surface MONITOR Not exposed as a command CONFIG GET/SET Not implemented — configuration is flags only

title: System commands
content:
System commands # The 110 commands in the command reference are the data surface. Under them sits a second surface, provided by the Raft/RESP layer, that operations depend on. It is not part of the Redis command set, so it is documented here.
None of these go through the Raft log unless stated, and --try-errors disables the CLUSTER family.
Connection # Command Reply Notes PING [message] PONG, or the message Handled before dispatch ECHO message the message — AUTH token OK / -unauthorized Required first when --auth is set QUIT OK, then the connection closes — SHUTDOWN (none — the process exits) Equivalent to SIGKILL from the client’s point of view; requires AUTH when configured Machine # Command Reply Meaning VERSION bulk string Engine version, e.g. 1.0.0-rc.1 MACHINE map of now, uptime, boottime (nanoseconds) Times come from the Raft clock, so every node agrees MACHINE HUMAN same keys as RFC3339 / duration Human-readable variant BARRIER OK A no-op write: when it returns, every previously issued write from this client has been applied BARRIER is how you get a read-your-writes guarantee across clients or nodes: send BARRIER on the leader, then read on a follower with --openreads.
RAFT # Command Reply Meaning RAFT HELP list of commands — RAFT LEADER address Advertised address of the current leader RAFT INFO [pattern] status map Raft state, term, applied/committed index, leader, peers RAFT SERVER LIST array of id, address, leader Cluster membership RAFT SERVER ADD id address 1 Add (or promote) a voter; address is what peers dial RAFT SERVER REMOVE id 1 Remove a member RAFT SNAPSHOT NOW snapshot id Take a snapshot immediately RAFT SNAPSHOT LIST array of id/size Snapshots on this node RAFT SNAPSHOT FILE id absolute path Where the snapshot file lives on the server RAFT SNAPSHOT READ id [RANGE offset limit] bulk bytes Read the file, whole or in windows redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SERVER LIST 1) 1) "id" 2) "1" 3) "address" 4) "127.0.0.1:11001" 5) "leader" 6) "true" ... redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SERVER ADD 4 10.0.0.14:11001 redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT SERVER REMOVE 4 Membership operations only succeed on the leader; on a follower they fail with the usual redirect error.
CLUSTER # Redis-cluster-shaped introspection, so that cluster-aware clients and proxies can discover topology:
Command Reply Meaning CLUSTER INFO multi-line string cluster_state:ok|fail, cluster_known_nodes, cluster_size, … CLUSTER NODES multi-line string One line per member: id, host:port@port, role (master/slave), leader id, connected, slots CLUSTER SLOTS array One range covering 0-16383 pointing at the leader The whole keyspace is reported as a single slot range on the leader, because there is no sharding. The point of these commands is compatibility, not distribution — a client that sees 0-16383 on one master behaves correctly, and every node holds every key anyway.
TICK (internal) # TICK <timestamp> <seed> is registered as a write command, replicated through the log, and used by the engine itself to advance the machine clock and random seed. The handler rejects malformed calls, but clients have no reason to send it: the Raft layer injects one every tick interval (default 200 ms), and that is what keeps m.Now() and m.Rand() identical across replicas. Write commands are required to use those two functions instead of time.Now()/math/rand for exactly this reason — see COMMAND-AUDIT.md in the repository.
Using the admin surface safely # Wrap admin commands in your own tooling; they take real arguments (RAFT SERVER REMOVE <id> is destructive) and there is no confirmation step. CLUSTER disappears when --try-errors is set, so do not build automation on it for a deployment that needs that flag. The surface is protected only by the shared --auth token. See Security.

title: Compatibility
content:
Compatibility with Redis # IceFireDB speaks RESP and most commands behave as Redis does, but it is not Redis: the storage model underneath is ledis, which keeps one keyspace per data type and stores expirations in whole seconds. This page lists the differences a client will actually notice, and why they exist.
Behaviours marked locked by test are pinned by compat_test.go (make test-compat) so they cannot change without a deliberate update.
1. No WRONGTYPE — one keyspace per data type # Redis: a key holds one value of one type; the wrong-type command fails with WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value.
IceFireDB keeps a separate keyspace per type (string, hash, list, set, sorted set). Consequences:
The same key name can hold a string and a hash and a list simultaneously. A type-mismatched command does not fail; it operates on that type’s own (possibly empty) view. There is no TYPE command at all, so you cannot ask which type a key currently has. SET k v -> OK HSET k f x -> 1 # Redis: WRONGTYPE, here: fine GET k -> "v" HGET k f -> "x" If your application relies on WRONGTYPE for type safety, enforce it in the application (for example with a key-naming convention such as user:1:profile vs user:1:fields).
locked by test — compat_test.go.
2. Expiration is per type # There is no single TTL per key. Each type has its own:
Type Expiry commands PERSIST String EXPIRE, EXPIREAT, TTL none (handler not registered) Hash HEXPIRE, HEXPIREAT, HTTL none (handler not registered) List LEXPIRE, LEXPIREAT, LTTL none (handler not registered) Set SEXPIRE, SEXPIREAT, STTL SPERSIST (the only one) Sorted set none — A sorted set cannot be given a TTL; clear it (ZCLEAR) and recreate, or keep the expiry in a string key. EXPIRE takes exactly KEY seconds — the Redis NX/XX/GT/LT options are not supported.
3. Expiration has one-second resolution # Expirations are stored as whole seconds, so SET key value PX 500 keeps the key for 1 second and PX 1500 for 2 (Redis: 0.5 s and 1.5 s). A key never expires earlier than requested, and every *TTL reports whole seconds.
4. Empty values collapse on the decentralized backends # HSET k f "" then HGET k f:
on goleveldb, badger, hybriddb: empty bulk string, as Redis; on the decentralized drivers: nil — “empty” and “absent” look the same. GET follows the same rule for string values. Do not store empty strings when “missing” must be distinguishable; store a sentinel or use a hash field’s presence.
5. Scan cursors are not integers # SCAN answers an opaque base64 cursor carrying five sub-cursors (one per keyspace). HSCAN/SSCAN/ZSCAN answer the last field or member name, so a field literally named 0 collides with the end marker. Client helpers that parse the cursor as an integer (go-redis’ typed HScan) reject it; use the generic command API. COUNT is capped at 10000, and a page may be empty while the cursor still advances. See Scan.
6. Expiration timestamps use the Raft clock # Every expiry is computed from the Raft machine clock (m.Now()), which keeps it identical on every replica, while the storage layer validates timestamps and reports TTL against the local wall clock. So:
when the Raft clock lags local time, a short-lived key can report TTL -1 although it still has a value; an expiry shorter than the clock skew is rejected with invalid expire value; TTL/HTTL/LTTL/STTL on different replicas can differ by their apply latency. Long TTLs are unaffected in practice. Do not build sub-second semantics on top of this.
7. Conditional writes see the local expiry check # Expired keys are reaped asynchronously against the local clock, and SET … NX/XX (and SETNX) test existence through that same view. A key that has logically expired may still be visible on one replica and not another, so two replicas can disagree about whether the write happens.
8. List rebuilds are not transactional # LINSERT and LREM have no storage primitive, so the handler rebuilds the list (LRange → LClear → RPush, then restores the TTL). The rebuild happens inside one Raft apply, so no other client sees a partial list, but a backend failure halfway leaves the list truncated. Both are O(n).
9. Three sorted-set commands do not replicate # ZINCRBY, ZREMRANGEBYRANK and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE are registered as read commands, so they mutate only the node that receives them. In a cluster that means no replication and no survival across a leader change. Use ZADD with a computed score and ZREM until this is fixed.
10. Bounded requests # Two client-supplied numbers are bounded so one request cannot materialise an unbounded reply:
Limit Value On violation COUNT on any scan 10000 Clamped (still a hint) ` count onSRANDMEMBER` SET … EX that would overflow int64 — Error reply, the write is refused Missing commands # Commands people reach for that this engine does not register:
Command Instead SELECT Nothing — one logical database TYPE Track the type yourself; keyspaces are per type KEYS SCAN 0 MATCH pattern COUNT n (or XSCAN) DBSIZE SCAN and count, or track it in the application MULTI/EXEC/WATCH No transactions; BARRIER gives read-your-writes BLPOP/BRPOP Poll with LPOP, or use a separate queue system MONITOR Not exposed CONFIG GET/SET Command-line flags only; restart to change them PERSIST (string), HPERSIST, LPERSIST EXPIRE again, or delete and rewrite ZEXPIRE/ZTTL, ZPOPMIN/ZPOPMAX ZCLEAR, ZRANGE/ZREM Scope of this page # This is not an exhaustive compatibility report; it captures the divergences confirmed to date. If you find another, it is worth a test in compat_test.go so it stops being accidental.

title: Overview
content:
What IceFireDB is # IceFireDB is a database infrastructure project that bridges web2 and web3 storage. This site documents the component that lives in the repository root and builds the IceFireDB binary — the NoSQL engine: a Redis-compatible server whose writes are replicated through a Raft log and whose data lives in a pluggable KV driver.
The two axes are independent, and that is the whole design:
Consistency axis — a Raft cluster inside one site (or one availability zone). A leader accepts writes, followers replay the log, --openreads lets followers serve reads. Storage axis — a store.driver.IDB implementation behind the ledis data model. It can be a local LSM engine, an object store, or a P2P replicated store. The command layer does not know which. Everything else — the RESP surface, the per-type keyspaces, expiration, snapshots — is layered on top of those two.
redis-cli / any RESP client │ ▼ RESP server (uhaha + redcon) ← pipelining, TLS, AUTH, CLUSTER/RAFT commands │ ▼ Raft log (hashicorp/raft) ← write commands are replayed on every replica │ ▼ command handlers (strings/hashes/lists/sets/zsets/scan) │ ▼ ledis data model (one keyspace per type) │ ▼ driver.IDB → goleveldb | badger | hybriddb | oss | ipfs | ipfs-synckv | crdt | ipfs-log Product map # Component What it is Where it runs NoSQL engine (this docs section) RESP server, Raft replication, pluggable KV storage repository root, binary IceFireDB IceFireDB-PubSub Redis PubSub protocol over a libp2p network IceFireDB-PubSub/ IceFireDB-SQLite MySQL protocol in front of a P2P-synchronised SQLite file IceFireDB-SQLite/ IceFireDB-SQLProxy MySQL proxy that replicates statements to MySQL backends IceFireDB-SQLProxy/ IceFireDB-Redis-Proxy RESP proxy that replicates commands to Redis backends IceFireDB-Redis-Proxy/ The NoSQL engine is the only component documented as a database engine here; the four proxies are middleware and are documented with their own configuration files.
What is implemented today # Capability State Evidence in the source RESP command surface 110 commands registered strings.go, hashes.go, lists.go, set.go, sorted_sets.go, scan.go, servers.go Raft replication + snapshots Working, integration-tested vendor/github.com/tidwall/uhaha, snapshot.go, integration_test.go Local storage goleveldb (default), badger, hybriddb driver/ + ledis store/goleveldb Object storage oss (S3-compatible) driver/oss Decentralized storage ipfs, ipfs-synckv, crdt, ipfs-log driver/ipfs*, driver/crdt, driver/ipfs-log TLS + cluster auth token Working --tls-cert, --tls-key, --auth / ICEFIREDB_AUTH Observability /healthz, /readyz, /metrics, INFO, optional pprof observability.go, server_info.go OrbitDB driver Disabled (commented out of main.go/flags.go) repository root Multi-database / SELECT Not implemented — one logical database COMMAND-REFERENCE.md Vector search, NATS messaging Not implemented in this engine — Where the rest of the documentation goes # Getting started — build, run, first commands, three-node cluster. Deployment — configuration, clustering, storage backends, security, observability, operations. Command reference — every registered command, plus the Raft/CLUSTER system commands. Architecture — protocol, network, storage and codec layers as they are built. Develop — clients, building, testing, benchmarking, ecosystem libraries.

title: Getting started
content:
Getting started # This page takes you from a clean checkout to a running node, then to a three-node cluster, and ends at the two things that surprise people first when they move from Redis.
Prerequisites # Go 1.27.3+. The module declares go 1.26.0 with toolchain go1.27.3, and CI builds and tests on Go 1.27.3. make (optional — every target is a thin go build). A RESP client: redis-cli is enough for everything except typed scan helpers (see Compatibility). 1. Build # git clone https://github.com/IceFireDB/IceFireDB.git cd IceFireDB make localbuild # → ./bin/IceFireDB make localbuild is go build -ldflags "-X main.BuildVersion=<git sha> -X main.BuildDate=<date>". make all cross-compiles the release matrix (linux amd64/arm64/armv5/armv6/armv7) — useful for releases, unnecessary while developing; make run and make run_dev simply go run ..
2. Run one node # ./bin/IceFireDB -a 127.0.0.1:11001 -n 1 -d ./data -l info That is every default explicitly: the bind address is 127.0.0.1:11001, the node ID is 1, the data directory is data, the log level is info. The binary prints a banner, then start with Storage Engine: goleveldb, then the Raft section of the log.
State is written under a per-node directory, so several nodes can share one -d:
data/ └── IceFireDB/ └── 1/ ├── main.db/ # the ledis storage (driver-dependent) ├── store/ # Raft log + stable store (leveldb or bolt, see --raft-backend) └── snapshots/ # Raft snapshots, one directory per snapshot ID 3. First commands # redis-cli -p 11001 127.0.0.1:11001> SET user:1 '{"name":"ada"}' EX 300 OK 127.0.0.1:11001> GET user:1 "{\"name\":\"ada\"}" 127.0.0.1:11001> TTL user:1 (integer) 299 127.0.0.1:11001> HSET user:1 name ada (integer) 1 127.0.0.1:11001> HGET user:1 name "ada" 127.0.0.1:11001> INFO $... Note line 4: the same key user:1 holds a string and a hash at the same time. That is not a bug — see step 5.
4. A three-node cluster # Node 1 is the bootstrap node; nodes 2 and 3 join it with -j. Every node keeps its own -d (you can also share the parent directory, the node ID keeps them apart).
# node 1 — bootstrap ./bin/IceFireDB -a 127.0.0.1:11001 -n 1 -d ./data & # node 2 — join ./bin/IceFireDB -a 127.0.0.1:11002 -n 2 -d ./data -j 127.0.0.1:11001 & # node 3 — join ./bin/IceFireDB -a 127.0.0.1:11003 -n 3 -d ./data -j 127.0.0.1:11001 & Check the topology from any node:
redis-cli -p 11001 CLUSTER INFO redis-cli -p 11001 CLUSTER NODES redis-cli -p 11001 RAFT LEADER Write to the leader, read from a follower:
redis-cli -p 11001 SET cluster:smoke ok # leader → OK redis-cli -p 11002 GET cluster:smoke # follower → -MOVED error unless --openreads A follower without --openreads answers a redirect error rather than stale data; add --openreads when you want follower reads. Membership, snapshots and failure handling are covered in Clustering.
5. Two things that are not Redis # There is no WRONGTYPE. The engine keeps a separate keyspace per data type, so SET k v and HSET k f x can both succeed, and a command for the wrong type reads that type’s own (possibly empty) view instead of failing. If your application depends on WRONGTYPE for type safety, check types at the application layer. Scan cursors are opaque, and for HSCAN they are names. Client helpers that parse the cursor as an integer (go-redis’ typed HScan, for example) do not work; use the generic command API. Both, plus eight more divergences, are in Compatibility.
Where next # Configuration — the full flag set with defaults, including TLS, auth, metrics and pprof. Command reference — 110 engine commands plus the RAFT/CLUSTER system commands. Clients — copy-pasteable examples for redis-cli, Go, Python and Node. Operations — backup, restore, rolling upgrade, health checks.

title: Deployment
content:
Deployment # Everything needed to run the NoSQL engine in production, in the order you will need it:
Page Questions it answers Configuration Which flags exist, what do they default to, which are inert? Clustering How does the Raft cluster work; how do I add/remove/replace a node? Storage backends Which driver should I choose; what does each one guarantee? Security TLS, the cluster auth token, and what is not protected. Observability /healthz, /readyz, /metrics, INFO sections, pprof. Operations Backup, restore, rolling upgrade, disaster recovery. System commands RAFT …, CLUSTER …, MACHINE, BARRIER, TICK, AUTH. Two properties hold across all of it and are worth stating once:
One data directory per node. The storage backend, the Raft log and the snapshots all live under <data-dir>/IceFireDB/<node-id>/. Copying that directory is a coherent backup primitive; changing the backend under an existing directory is not supported. The admin surface is opt-in and loopback-bound. --metrics and --pprof are off by default, and when enabled they listen on 127.0.0.1 unless you pass an address.

title: Command reference
content:
Command reference # Every command the engine registers, grouped by data type. The table below is the whole surface: 110 commands, plus the system commands (RAFT, CLUSTER, MACHINE, BARRIER, AUTH, …) that the Raft/RESP layer answers.
Page Commands Count Strings SET … BITPOS, expiry 26 Hashes HSET … HMCLEAR, expiry 19 Lists LPUSH … LREM, expiry 18 Sets SADD … SPERSIST 21 Sorted sets ZADD … ZCLEAR 15 Scan SCAN/HSCAN/SSCAN/ZSCAN + the X* family 8 Server INFO, FLUSHALL, FLUSHDB 3 Compatibility divergences from Redis, with reasons — Notation # Notation Meaning KEY Binary-safe key name, up to 1024 bytes (ledis MaxKeySize; empty keys are rejected) VALUE Binary-safe value, up to 1 GiB (MaxValueSize) [ARG] Optional argument ARG... One or more repetitions A | B Alternative R / W Read command (runs locally) / write command (replicated through the Raft log) integer RESP integer :1 bulk RESP bulk string $3 foo null RESP null bulk $-1, “no such value” array RESP array *2 … +OK RESP simple string Rules that apply to every command # One keyspace per data type. A key can hold a string and a hash and a list at the same time. A command for the wrong type operates on that type’s own (possibly empty) view instead of answering WRONGTYPE. See Compatibility. Expiration is per type. EXPIRE/TTL apply to the string; HEXPIRE/HTTL to the hash; LEXPIRE/LTTL to the list; SEXPIRE/STTL/SPERSIST to the set. Sorted sets have no TTL command. TTLs are whole seconds; -1 means “no expiration” and is also what an expired key reports. Scores are 64-bit integers, not floats. Counts and paging are bounded. COUNT is capped at 10000, |count| on SRANDMEMBER at 1048576. Writes are replayed on every replica, so their result must be identical cluster-wide — that is why e.g. SPOP picks deterministically. Errors are RESP errors (-ERR …). -WRONGTYPE is never produced. A follower that may not serve a read answers -MOVED (or -TRY with --try-errors). Read/write classes, and why they matter # R means the handler is registered with conf.AddReadCommand: it executes on the node that receives it, against whatever state that node has applied. W means conf.AddWriteCommand: it is serialised through the Raft log and applied on every node.
Three sorted-set commands are registered as reads although they mutate:
Command Registered as Effect in a cluster ZINCRBY R Mutates the local node only — not replicated, lost on leader change ZREMRANGEBYRANK R Same ZREMRANGEBYSCORE R Same Until that changes, use ZADD with a computed score, and delete members with ZREM.
Reply types # Handlers return Go values that the RESP layer maps directly:
Handler returns Client sees nil null bulk ($-1) []byte bulk string [][]byte, []string array redcon.SimpleString simple string (+OK) redcon.SimpleInt, int64 integer error error reply (-ERR …) A simple string cannot carry \r\n, so values are never returned as one.
Limits # Limit Value Key size 1024 bytes (ledis.MaxKeySize); an empty key is rejected Hash field / set member / zset member 1024 bytes each Value size 1 GiB (ledis.MaxValueSize) COUNT on any scan 10000, clamped; still only a hint SRANDMEMBER / SPOP count absolute value ≤ 1048576; SPOP clamps to set size Expiration whole seconds; PX rounds up; unrepresentable EX is refused Databases 1 (SELECT unimplemented) Blocking commands none (BLPOP/BRPOP are not registered)

title: Architecture
content:
Architecture # How the binary is put together, layer by layer, as it exists in this tree — not as it was once planned.
Page Layer Overview Startup sequence, request path, what runs where Protocol RESP server, pipelining, reply mapping, cluster redirects Network Raft transport, peer discovery, the P2P drivers Storage ledis data model, per-type keyspaces, TTLs, snapshots Codec How five data types become KV operations RESP client ──► uhaha/redcon ──► Raft log ──► handlers ──► ledis ──► driver.IDB │ (leader) (110 cmds) (types) (8 drivers) └── AUTH / PING / QUIT / RAFT / CLUSTER / MACHINE / BARRIER Two boundaries are worth holding in mind while reading the rest of this site:
The Raft layer owns ordering, not semantics. It decides when a write applies; the handler decides what it means. Everything that must be identical on every replica (randomness, time) is injected by the Raft layer and consumed by handlers through m.Now() and m.Rand(). The storage driver owns durability, not structure. It stores opaque key/value pairs. Every structure — a hash, a list, a score index — is encoded by ledis above the driver, which is why the same data model works on LevelDB and on IPFS.

title: FAQ
content:
Frequently asked questions # Is it a Redis replacement? # It speaks RESP and implements 110 commands with Redis semantics for most of them, so a Redis client connects without changes. But it is not a drop-in Redis: there is no WRONGTYPE, no SELECT, no transactions, no blocking commands, keys are limited to 1024 bytes, and three sorted-set commands do not replicate. Read Compatibility before migrating anything you care about.
Which commands are supported? # 110 data commands plus the RAFT/CLUSTER/MACHINE/BARRIER/AUTH system commands. The full list is in the command reference, one page per data type, with reply types and limits.
Why does INFO memory fail? # Because INFO takes no arguments in this engine. Use INFO and parse the # Mem section out of the reply. See Observability.
Why is there no WRONGTYPE error? # Because the storage model keeps one keyspace per data type, so a key name can hold a string, a hash and a list at once, and a wrong-type command operates on that type’s own view. There is also no TYPE command, so type safety is the application’s job. Pinned by compat_test.go.
Why did my HSCAN in Go/Python fail with a parse error? # Because HSCAN/SSCAN/ZSCAN use the last field or member name as the cursor, not a number, and the typed client helpers coerce the cursor to int. Use the generic command API (Do, execute_command). SCAN’s own cursor is opaque base64 and is fine with Scan-style helpers. See Scan.
How do I configure it? # Command-line flags only — there is no config file. --storage-backend, -a, -n, -d, -j, --auth, --tls-cert/--tls-key, --metrics, --pprof, the driver flags. The complete set with defaults is in Configuration.
Is --hot-cache-size a real flag? # No. It is printed by -h but not registered, so passing it is an error and the cache capacity stays at the driver default (1024 MB). See flags that are printed but not wired.
Which storage backend should I use? # goleveldb unless you have a reason. badger for heavier local writes, hybriddb for read-heavy working sets, oss when data must outlive the host, ipfs-synckv/crdt for multi-site P2P. The ipfs driver is not usable as a general backend today. See Storage backends.
How do I scale reads? # Add nodes and run with --openreads so followers serve reads, or point a proxy at the followers. There is no sharding: every node stores the full dataset. See Clustering.
How do I back up and restore? # RAFT SNAPSHOT NOW then copy RAFT SNAPSHOT FILE <id>, or copy a quiesced node directory. Restore with --restore <file> into a fresh data directory, then re-join the other nodes. Details and caveats in Operations.
Can I restore a badger backup into a goleveldb node? # Yes for a snapshot (state.bin is a backend-independent key/value stream). No for a copied data directory — main.db/ is backend-specific and you must never change --storage-backend for an existing data directory.
Why did a follower return -MOVED 0 <addr>? # Because without --openreads, followers refuse reads and redirect to the leader. Slot 0 is used for all keys; there is no sharding. With --try-errors the same reply becomes -TRY.
Where did my write go in a cluster? # If it was ZINCRBY, ZREMRANGEBYRANK or ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, nowhere: those three are registered as read commands, so they mutate only the node you sent them to. Use ZADD with a computed score and ZREM.
Why can’t I use keys longer than 1024 bytes? # Because ledis enforces 1 KiB keys, fields and set/zset members (values may be up to 1 GiB). It is a storage-layer limit, not a policy. Keep keys compact and hash long identifiers client-side.
Is it production ready? # The engine ships as 1.0.0-rc.1. Local backends (goleveldb, badger, hybriddb), Raft replication, snapshots, TLS/auth and observability are exercised by CI (including crash-recovery, failover and partition tests). The decentralized drivers vary: ipfs-synckv is tested, crdt/ipfs-log are not unit-tested here, and ipfs cannot round-trip values. Own the risk accordingly.
Is there authentication, and is it per user? # There is one shared token (--auth or ICEFIREDB_AUTH), required on every connection and shared by all nodes. No users, roles, or per-command permissions. Pair it with TLS. See Security.
Does it support transactions, pub/sub, streams or SQL? # Not in this binary. MULTI/EXEC, pub/sub, streams and SQL are not implemented; pub/sub is a separate binary ( IceFireDB-PubSub) and SQL support lives in IceFireDB-SQLite/ SQLProxy.
What license is it under? # Apache 2.0 for the engine; the PubSub component is MIT. See LICENSE in each directory.
Where do I report a bug? # github.com/IceFireDB/IceFireDB/issues. A reproduction against make run plus the INFO output and the backend in use gets triaged fastest.

title: IceFireDB-PubSub
content:
IceFireDB-PubSub # Redis PubSub protocol over a libp2p network: clients keep using SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH, and the messages travel between nodes across NATs and regions instead of staying inside one Redis instance.
cd IceFireDB-PubSub make # → bin/IceFireDB-PubSub ./bin/IceFireDB-PubSub -c ./config/config.yaml redis-cli -p 16379 SUBSCRIBE name # terminal 1 redis-cli -p 16379 PUBLISH name hello # terminal 2 (any node in the mesh) What it is # Property Value Protocol Redis RESP — SUBSCRIBE, UNSUBSCRIBE, PSUBSCRIBE, PUBLISH Transport between nodes libp2p pubsub (Kademlia DHT + IPFS-network discovery) Local listener proxy.local_port, default 16379 Binary bin/IceFireDB-PubSub (-c <config.yaml>) State No persistence: this is a message bus, not a database Configuration (config/config.yaml) # Key Meaning Default in file proxy.local_port RESP listener 16379 proxy.enable_mtls Mutual TLS between proxies false p2p.enable Turn the libp2p mesh on true p2p.service_discovery_id Rendezvous name — must match across peers p2p_redis_proxy_service_test p2p.service_command_topic Command channel inside the mesh p2p_redis_proxy_service_topic_test p2p.service_discover_mode advertise or announce advertise p2p.node_host_ip / node_host_port Address peers should use (0 = any port) 127.0.0.1 / 0 pprof_debug.enable / .port /debug/pprof server true / 16060 log.level debug, info, warn, error debug ip_white_list.enable / .list Client IP allow-list true / loopback entries cache.enable / .max_items_size / .default_expiration (ms) / .cleanup_interval (s) Message cache true / 2048 / 5000 / 120 ignore_cmd.enable / .cmd_list Drop selected commands false / [] Notes that bite in real deployments:
The discovery id and command topic are the network identity. Copying the config from the sample without changing them puts your cluster in the same mesh as anyone else who did the same. pprof_debug is enabled and listens on 16060 in the sample config. Turn it off, or bind it to loopback and firewall it. The IP allow-list is enabled by default with 127.0.0.1, so a remote client is refused until you add its address. What it does not do # No message persistence, no replay, no consumer groups, no streams. No cross-mesh bridge: two different service_discovery_ids are two separate worlds. Not part of the NoSQL engine’s command surface — the engine has no SUBSCRIBE at all. Where it fits # Use it when web2 clients already publish through Redis and you want the bus to span sites without rewriting them. Pair it with a real queue if you need delivery guarantees; PubSub is best-effort by design.

title: IceFireDB-SQLite
content:
IceFireDB-SQLite # A MySQL-protocol server that stores data in a local SQLite file and propagates statements to peers, so every node can answer SQL queries against its own copy.
cd IceFireDB-SQLite make # → bin/IceFireDB-SQLite ./bin/IceFireDB-SQLite -c ./config/config.yaml mysql -h 127.0.0.1 -P 23306 -u root -p # password from userlist in the config What it is # Property Value Protocol MySQL wire protocol (MySQL clients, drivers, ORMs) Storage SQLite file, sqlite.filename Replication Statements propagated between peers over libp2p Listener server.addr, default :23306 Binary bin/IceFireDB-SQLite (-c <config.yaml>) Configuration (config/config.yaml) # Key Meaning Default in file server.addr MySQL listener ":23306" sqlite.filename SQLite database file db/sqlite.db debug.enable / .port pprof server false / 17878 p2p.enable P2P replication true p2p.service_discovery_id Rendezvous name, must match peers p2p_sqlite_service p2p.service_command_topic Command channel p2p_sqlite_service_topic p2p.service_discover_mode advertise or announce advertise p2p.node_host_ip / node_host_port Address peers should dial 127.0.0.1 / 0 userlist Tenant users: user + password root / 123456 Operational notes # The sample password is 123456. Change userlist before exposing the port — MySQL clients will happily connect with it. Statements are replayed on peers, so non-deterministic SQL (NOW(), RAND(), UUID()) can diverge between nodes. Keep statements deterministic, or accept drift. Each node holds a full copy in its own SQLite file; there is no sharding or leader election. Schema changes propagate like any other statement: run them at a quiet moment, not concurrently with writes. Relationship to the NoSQL engine # Different binary, different protocol, different consistency story: no Raft, no RESP, no shared storage driver. Use it when the application is SQL-shaped and per-node reads are the goal; use the NoSQL engine when you need Raft consistency and RESP.

title: IceFireDB-SQLProxy
content:
IceFireDB-SQLProxy # A MySQL-protocol proxy that sits in front of ordinary MySQL servers and replays statements to the other agents in the mesh, so several MySQL instances in different places stay in step without changing the application.
cd IceFireDB-SQLProxy make # → bin/IceFireDB-SQLProxy ./bin/IceFireDB-SQLProxy -c ./config/config.yaml mysql -h 127.0.0.1 -P 33306 -u host1 -p # a user from userlist What it is # Property Value Protocol MySQL wire protocol Backend MySQL (mysql.admin, mysql.readonly) Replication Statements propagated between agents over libp2p Listener server.addr, default :33306 Binary bin/IceFireDB-SQLProxy (-c <config.yaml>) Configuration (config/config.yaml) # Key Meaning Default in file server.addr Proxy listener ":33306" debug.enable / .port Debug/pprof server true / 17878 mysql.admin Write connection pool: addr, user, password, dbname, minAlive, maxAlive, maxIdle 127.0.0.1:3306, admin_user mysql.readonly Read connection pool, same keys 127.0.0.1:3306, readonly_user userlist Client tenants (user/password) host1 / host1 p2p.enable Mesh replication true p2p.serviceDiscoveryId Rendezvous name, must match peers tanovo_sqlproxy_admin_service p2p.serviceCommandTopic Command channel tanovo_sqlproxy_command_topic p2p.adminTopic / p2p.readonlyTopic Per-role channels tanovo_sqlproxy_admin_topic / …_readonly_topic p2p.serviceDiscoverMode advertise or announce advertise p2p.nodeHostIp / nodeHostPort Address peers should dial 127.0.0.1 / 0 Note the camelCase keys in this component (serviceDiscoveryId, not service_discovery_id as in PubSub/SQLite). Copying a config between components silently gives you a default value.
Operational notes # Read/write separation is a config choice, not routing magic: mysql.readonly is the pool used for read queries, mysql.admin for writes. Point them at the same server if you have no replica. Sample credentials (admin_pass, readonly_pass, host1/host1) are placeholders — replace them. Statements replay to every agent, so deterministic SQL only. NOW()/RAND()/UUID() can diverge. No conflict resolution: the mesh is ordered by arrival, so two agents writing the same row concurrently converge on whichever statement applies last. The debug server is enabled in the sample config on port 17878; turn it off in production. When to use it # You already run MySQL and want the same data available closer to users in other regions without moving the application to a new database. It is not a MySQL cluster replacement: it does not do automatic failover of the MySQL backend, and it does not guarantee cross-site consistency for conflicting writes.

title: IceFireDB-Redis-Proxy
content:
IceFireDB-Redis-Proxy # A RESP proxy in front of Redis (single node or cluster) that replays commands to the other agents in the mesh. Existing Redis applications get multi-site synchronisation without switching databases.
cd IceFireDB-Redis-Proxy make # → bin/IceFireDB-Redis-Proxy ./bin/IceFireDB-Redis-Proxy -c ./config/config.yaml redis-cli -p 16379 SET k v What it is # Property Value Protocol Redis RESP on both sides Backend redisdb.type: node or cluster, redisdb.start_nodes Replication Commands propagated between agents over libp2p Listener proxy.local_port, default 16379 Binary bin/IceFireDB-Redis-Proxy (-c <config.yaml>) Configuration (config/config.yaml) # Key Meaning Default in file proxy.local_port RESP listener 16379 proxy.enable_mtls Mutual TLS for the proxy listener false redisdb.type node or cluster node redisdb.start_nodes Comma-separated backend addresses 127.0.0.1:6379 redisdb.conn_timeout / conn_read_timeout / conn_write_timeout / conn_alive_timeout Seconds 5 / 1 / 1 / 60 redisdb.conn_pool_size Backend connections (0 = short-lived) 80 p2p.enable, service_discovery_id, service_command_topic, service_discover_mode, node_host_ip, node_host_port Mesh settings same shape as PubSub pprof_debug.enable / .port pprof server true / 16060 log.level Log level debug ip_white_list.enable / .list Client allow-list true / loopback cache.enable / .max_items_size / .default_expiration (ms) / .cleanup_interval (s) Proxy cache true / 2048 / 5000 / 120 ignore_cmd.enable / .cmd_list Commands to drop false / [] Operational notes # redisdb.start_nodes must point at a reachable backend before clients connect; the proxy is not a database and has no storage of its own. Commands are replayed on peers: non-deterministic ones (SPOP, INCRBYFLOAT, anything using server time, EVAL with math.random) will diverge across sites. Prefer deterministic operations, or keep those keys in one site. The cache in front of the backend defaults to enabled with a 5 s expiration — read-after-write from a different client can be stale for up to that window. Disable cache.enable when you need strict reads. pprof_debug is on in the sample config (16060); disable it outside development. Same discovery-id caveat as PubSub: two deployments with the same id share a mesh. Proxy or engine? # Need Use Keep existing Redis, add multi-site sync IceFireDB-Redis-Proxy Replace Redis with a Raft-replicated engine and pluggable storage NoSQL engine Only message fan-out IceFireDB-PubSub

title: Vocabulary
content:
Vocabulary # The main terms used in IceFireDB products are listed below.
Item describe NoSQL Non-relational databases, which store data in a format different from relational tables. LSM In computer science, the log-structured merge-tree (also known as LSM tree, or LSMT) is a data structure with performance characteristics that make it attractive for providing indexed access to files with high insert volume, such as transactional log data. OSS Object Storage Service IPFS The InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) is a protocol, hypermedia and file sharing peer-to-peer network for storing and sharing data in a distributed file system. P2P peer-to-peer network EVM Smart contracts A smart contract is a computer program or a transaction protocol that is intended to automatically execute, control or document legally-relevant events and actions according to the terms of a contract or an agreement. CRDT In distributed computing, a conflict-free replicated data type (CRDT) is a data structure that is replicated across multiple computers in a network, RAFT Raft is a consensus algorithm that is designed to be easy to understand. IPLD IPLD stands for InterPlanetary Linked Data,IPLD is an ecosystem of formats and data structures for building applications that can be fully decentralized. IPFS-LOG IPFS-log is an immutable, operation-based collision-free replication data structure (CRDT) for distributed systems. It is an append-only log that can be used to model the variable sharing state between peers in p2p applications.
